39.title: Epigastric Pain
39.chiefComplaint: Severe epigastric pain radiating to back, nausea, vomiting
39.caseSummary:
Differential: Distal aortic dissection, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, biliary disease, perforated bowel, intestinal obstruction, Cholelithiasis, Acute cholecystitis, Acute pancreatitis, Acute Hepatitis, Ascending Cholangitis and Biliary
Colic.

The patient has gallstone pancreatitis. This is evident by the patient's symptoms of pancreatitis including epigastric pain which radiates to the back, nausea/vomiting, as well as diagnostic test results of elevated lipase, and a
CT scan showing inflammation of the pancreas. There are many different causes of pancreatitis, but the two most common are alcohol use and gallstones. The patient is also jaundiced and has elevated LFTs, further indicating
biliary obstruction, The Ultrasound shows gallstones in the gallbladder, and dilation of the common bile duct and the CT shows blockage of the pancreatic ducts (ampulla of Vater) which caused the acute pancreatitis. The
patient should be treated aggressively with NPO, admission to the hospital (inpatient or ICU), IV fluids, IV pain medications/antiemetics as needed, and ERCP to remove the obstruction. Once the patient's inflammation has
decreased, and she has clinically improved, the patient should be scheduled for an elective cholecystectomy with a general surgeon to prevent further gallstone obstructions in the future.
39.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and low-grade fever. Exam reveals epigastric tenderness with guarding, jaundiced sclera, and possibly Grey Turner/Cullen signs in severe cases. Most common causes: gallstones (GET SMASHED mnemonic — Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps, Autoimmune, Scorpion stings, Hypercalcemia/Hypertriglyceridemia, ERCP, Drugs). Diagnosis requires 2 of 3: (1) characteristic epigastric pain, (2) lipase/amylase >3x upper limit, (3) CT findings. Lipase is more sensitive and specific than amylase (especially in delayed presentation). Ranson criteria and BISAP score for severity. Management: aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (LR preferred over NS), NPO initially, IV analgesics (morphine OK), antiemetics. Early enteral nutrition within 24-48h (NG or NJ feeds). ERCP within 24h if gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis or obstruction. CT with contrast at 48-72h if not improving to assess for necrosis/complications.

40.title: Chest Pain
40.chiefComplaint: Acute chest pain, palpitations, SOB, sense of impending doom
40.caseSummary:
Differential: Panic attack, Myocardial infarction, Anxiety, Hyperthyroidism, Substance abuse, Pheochromocytoma, Hypoglycemia, Asthma, Pulmonary embolus.

This patient has had a panic attack. She has a highly stressful job as an executive in a large corporation, Panic disorder is a diagnosis of exclusion, so medical problems that can cause panic attacks should be ruled out first,
such as hyperthyroidism, substance use, heart problems, pulmonary embolus, etc. Given that the patient is 26 and has no medical history with a normal EKG and labs, it is not necessary to do invasive and expensive tests such
asa Chest CT to rule out a pulmonary embolus. The patient reports that she has had similar attacks previously, so the concer for a cardiac event or pulmonary embolism is low. Acutely, the patient could be treated with a
benzodiazepine (optional) although first-line, long-term treatment for panic disorder would be SSRI therapy with or without concurrent cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). The patient would benefit from both a psychiatry

and psychology consult before discharge, and can then follow-up as an outpatient in 1-4 weeks time.

It can be argued that in real life that you should not start an SSRI/SNRI in the emergency room as they typically will just refer to their PCP. However, your role is different in the computer simulation. You are a generalist
physician who treats patients in a variety of settings. An official statement of your role taken directly from the USMLE: “ In the generalist role, you must manage your patient in both inpatient and outpatient settings.
Sometimes this may involve management in more than one location—initially caring for a patient in the emergency department, admitting the patient to the hospital, and discharging and following the patient in the
outpatient setting.” Essentially, you will see the patient in the ER and follow-up with them personally as an outpatient. Although this is not realistic, this is how you will be graded, so you should initiate SSRI/SNRI treatment in

the Emergency Room setting.

41.title: Generalized Weakness
41.chiefComplaint: Generalized weakness, cola-colored urine, periorbital/ankle edema
41.caseSummary:
Differential: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, membranoproliferative glomerular nephritis, Cryoglobulinemia, Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture syndrome), IgA nephropathy, Lupus.

This patient has had a poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). The patient had an upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago, that sounded like it was likely a group A streptococcal pharyngitis, but was not treated with
antibiotics. The most common timeframe for PSGN to develop is 10-14 days after infection, which was the timeframe we saw in this case. The patient had hematuria, edema, mild hypertension, low complement levels (low c3),
proteinuria, and a positive antistreptolysin-O. PSGN is usually self limited and typically resolves in weeks to months with a good prognosis. Treatment of PSGN is supportive, which in this case would include treating the
edema and hypertension with loop diuretics and an anti-hypertensive, such as nifedepine, plus salt and water restriction in addition to calling a nephrology consult. The use of antibiotics is controversial but points would not
be taken away if used. The difficult part of this case is to correctly rule out other causes of the patient's acute glomerulonephritis. This would include getting an ANCA, an ANA, anti-dsDNA, cryocrit, anti-GBM, and
complement (C3) levels. If these antibodies are all negative and C3 is low, then you can be assured that the diagnosis of PSGN is accurate. The patient should be followed up in 1 week time.
41.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a child who presents with generalized weakness, oliguria, cola-colored (dark brown) urine, periorbital and ankle edema (2+ pitting), and hypertension 1-4 weeks after a streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection (impetigo). This is acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis — an immune complex-mediated (type III hypersensitivity) disease. Antigen-antibody complexes deposit in the glomerular basement membrane → complement activation → glomerular inflammation. Labs: UA shows hematuria (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts — pathognomonic), proteinuria (<3.5g/day — nephritic, not nephrotic range). Low C3 complement (returns to normal in 6-8 weeks). Elevated ASO titer (pharyngitis) or anti-DNase B (skin infection). BMP shows elevated BUN/Cr (acute kidney injury). Diagnosis is clinical. Renal biopsy only if rapidly progressive GN or atypical course. Treatment: supportive — salt/fluid restriction, diuretics (furosemide) for hypertension and edema, antihypertensives if needed. Prognosis excellent in children (>95% complete recovery). Antibiotics if active strep infection. No immunosuppression needed.

42.title: Knee Pain
42.chiefComplaint: Acute severe knee pain, redness, swelling
42.caseSummary:
Differential: Gout, Bacterial arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, lyme disease, pseudogout, psoriatic arthritis.

This patient has an acute gout attack. To definitively diagnose the patient, it is important to get an arthrocentesis and analyze the synovial fluid to look for crystals and rule out infectious causes that could cause monoarticular
pain. The patient has needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals in the synovial fluid which confirms the diagnosis of gout. If the crystals were calcium pyrophosphate crystals (which are weakly positively
birefringent, rod-shaped and rhomboidal shaped crystals), then the patient would have pseudogout. The patient has a fever, so infectious etiology is on the differential. Doing a urethral culture/gram stain, lyme serology are
all indicated to rule out other causes. NSAIDs are the treatment of choice for the patient. Corticosteroids or colchicine are also acceptable. The patient's chlorthalidone should be discontinued because thiazide diuretics
increase serum uric acid levels and can precipitate a gout attack (although when tested during an acute flare may be normal or even low). The patient also states that he drank a lot of alcohol recently which also could
precipitate a gout attack. The patient should be switched to another antihypertensive agent such as an ACE inhibitor like Lisinopril or a calcium channel blocker, like amlodipine. The patient should be counseled to limit his
alcohol intake, limit his purine intake (such as meats), and to hydrate appropriately. In a followup visit in 1-2 weeks, the patient could be put on a prophylactic regimen of allopurinol since the patient's 24-hour urine uric acid
level is above 800mg. However, since this is the first attack and there were multiple factors that could have caused the high uric acid (beer, thiazide diuretic), it would also be reasonable to wait to see if the patient has another
attack before starting him on a prophylactic medication. A discussion with the patient would be warranted,

Pain began suddenly overnight — classic podagra (great toe) or knee involvement. History reveals dietary triggers (red meat, seafood, alcohol) or diuretic use. Gout is caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints from chronic hyperuricemia. Definitive diagnosis: joint aspiration with synovial fluid analysis under polarized light microscopy — needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. Do NOT give NSAIDs in renal impairment. First-line acute treatment: NSAIDs (indomethacin or naproxen), colchicine (within 36h of onset), or corticosteroids (oral prednisone or intra-articular injection). Colchicine: avoid in renal/hepatic impairment, CYP3A4 interactions. Long-term urate-lowering: allopurinol or febuxostat (start after acute flare resolves, with colchicine prophylaxis for 3-6 months). Target uric acid <6.0 mg/dL (or <5.0 for tophaceous gout).

43.title: Knee Pain
43.caseSummary:
Differential: Acute HIV infection, Secondary syphilis, Viral infections (Parvovirus B19, measles, rubella, arbovirus), gout, pseudogout, Lyme disease.

The patient has septic arthritis from a Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection that she likely picked up in Mexico on her recent vacation. The patient's recent sexual contacts, followed by dysuria and pustules and now fevers, chills,
and tachycardia leads you to think that the patient has a disseminated N. gonorroeae infection. The patient's synovial fluid from her L knee arthrocentesis showed a high amount of WBC with some gram negative diplococci
which strongly favors a N. gonorrhoeae diagnosis, although urogenital specimens should be obtained and tested, She should also be tested for other sexually transmitted infections including chlamydia, syphilis, HIV, hepatitis
B and hepatitis C. The patient meets SIRS criteria on initial presentation (fever >38C, tachycardia > 100bpm), so she should be treated in the ED or inpatient unit of the hospital. Blood and urine cultures should be obtained
before starting her on antibiotics immediately. First-line treatment for disseminated gonococcal infection is IV ceftriaxone. Cefotaxime and ceftizoxime are alternative options. It is important to give a 1 time dose of
azithromycin to treat for C. trachomatis co-infection or use doxycycline. The patient's sexual partner(s) should receive treatment as well

You can treat her pain and fever with ibuprofen or acetaminophen. The patient will begin to feel better in 1-2 days, and the case will end. In real life, the patient can be continued on oral antibiotics for another 1-2 weeks to.

assure that the bacterial infection is cleared. The patient should also be educated on safe sex practices, smoking cessation, and given a warning to avoid illicit drugs.

Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) is the most common cause of septic arthritis in sexually active young adults. Classic triad: tenosynovitis, dermatitis (pustular or vesiculopustular lesions), and migratory polyarthralgia progressing to monoarticular septic arthritis. Most commonly affects knee. Joint drainage (serial aspiration or arthroscopy). Partner treatment essential.

44.title: Diarrhea
44.chiefComplaint: Chronic foul-smelling greasy diarrhea, bloating, weight loss
44.caseSummary:
Differential: Giardiasis, Amebiasis, Infectious diarrhea (including bacterial, viral, parasitic), Inflammatory bowel disease, food poisoning, gastroenteritis, Hepatitis A, C. difficile infection, irritable bowel syndrome.

The patient has Giardia likely from his recent trip to Mexico with his friends. Other infectious causes of diarrhea should be ruled out by getting stool cultures, analyzing stool microscopy for ova and parasites and getting a
stool C. diff study. Because of the acute nature of the symptoms and recent travel history, non-infectious causes such as inflammatory bowel disease or irritable bowel syndrome are less likely. The giardia stool antigen comes
back positive and stool microscopy showed Giardia protozoa, so the diagnosis is confirmed. Because the patient has vital signs within normal limits, normal chemistries and a normal CBC, he can be treated as an outpatient.

The patient will then need treatment with metronidazole or other antiparasitic agent, and the patient will begin to feel better, and the case will end. The patient should be counseled for adequate hydration and counsel
against binge drinking, and would benefit from avoiding alcohol altogether while taking metronidazole, given the disulfiram-like reaction it can cause if taken with alcohol.
44.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea (steatorrhea), bloating, abdominal cramps, and weight loss. History reveals recent camping/hiking trip drinking untreated stream water. Giardia lamblia is a flagellated protozoan transmitted via fecal-oral route through contaminated water (common in hikers/campers — 'beaver fever'). Cysts are chlorine-resistant. Diagnosis: stool O&P (ova and parasites) — multiple samples needed (shedding intermittent). Stool Giardia antigen ELISA is more sensitive. String test (Entero-Test) if stool studies negative. Treatment: tinidazole (single dose) or metronidazole (5-7 days). Nitazoxanide for children. Paromomycin in pregnancy. Treat close contacts. Boil or filter water when camping.

45.title: Unresponsive
45.caseSummary:
Differential: Narcotic overdose, TCA overdose, Aspirin overdose, toxic alcohol ingestion, ethanol poisoning, acetaminophen overdose, other medication overdose.

This patient overdosed on opioids in an apparent suicide attempt. The patient had a recent life stressor (end of a relationship) and had access to narcotics that were either prescribed to her for her fibromyalgia or prescribed
to one of her family members or friends. Opioid intoxication is often a clinical diagnosis; naloxone should be empirically administered to any unresponsive patient, but this patient had several clues that pointed to this
toxidrome, specifically the pinpoint pupils (miosis) and decreased respiratory rate. Naloxone is a short-acting opioid antagonist that is preferably given IV but can be administered nasally, subcutaneously, or intramuscularly if
IV access cannot be obtained. Due to its short half-life and depending on the amount of opioids ingested or injected, patients can again become unresponsive or depress their respiratory rates after initial naloxone
administration, so it might need to be administered several times for sustained clinical improvement. Acute management of the unresponsive patient with suspected overdose includes obtaining a pulse oximetry, EKG and
cardiac monitoring, and IV access.

Although results of lab tests should not delay administration of naloxone, one should obtain basic labs (CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, urinalysis, ABG) in addition to those specific for suspected overdose (urine tox
screen, acetaminophen level, salicylates, TCA level, lactate, ethanol level and toxic alcohol panel). The patient should be admitted to the inpatient setting, put on suicide precautions, and be seen by a psychiatry consult once
medically stabilized, who may decide to start her on psychiatric medications to help manage her mood symptoms. Activated charcoal should be administered when the patient is awake and responsive. Activated charcoal is
given in case the patient overdosed on any other substances or prescription medications which would prevent absorption of these things. There may be a concern that the patient overdosed on combination opioids (Le.
acetaminophen-hydrocodone), and the patient has not absorbed enough to cause symptoms or lab changes. Gastric lavage and NG tubes are not commonly used anymore in overdose. Activated charcoal is not given to
sedative patients via NG tubes because the patient is not protecting their own airway, and they can aspirate charcoal which can cause pneumonitis. Activated charcoal is best used if the patient ingested recently (<2 hours).
However, if it is an unknown ingestion at an unknown time, then giving activated charcoal is indicated (if the patient is alert/awake enough to swallow it as aforementioned). Psychiatry should be consulted, and the patient
should be put on suicide precautions and monitored for at least 24 hours before discharge to a psychiatric facility or to home depending on the results of the psychiatry consult.

46.title: Weakness in Extremities
46.caseSummary:
Differential: Guillain-Barre Syndrome, Myasthenia gravis, Paraneoplastic neuropathy, HIV peripheral neuropathy, Conversion disorder, Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, Acute myelopathy (from
compression, transverse myelitis, vascular injury), Toxic neuropathies, West Nile encephalitis.

The patient has Guillain-Barre Syndrome, an immune-mediated polyneuropathy usually triggered by a preceding infection. The most notorious infection is Campylobacter jejuni, bacteria which can cause an acute diarrheal
illness. C. jejuni has proteins that mimic the myelin surrounding nerves, so when the body produces antibodies against these proteins to fight the bacterial infection, they can also attack the myelin around nerves, causing a
demyelinating syndrome (also known as “molecular mimicry’). The demyelination causes progressive, typically symmetric ascending muscle weakness. Given the patient's reported difficulty breathing (despite stable vital signs
and pulse oximetry) this is a red flag for impending respiratory muscle involvement and possible respiratory failure, so he should be urgently admitted for further workup and management. The patient should get lab work
done, including a lumbar puncture and CSF analyses, to rule out other causes of muscle weakness and polyneuropathy. Electrodiagnostic studies (EMG, nerve conduction studies), in addition to the clinical history and exam,
will help make the diagnosis of GBS. Spinal MRI may be helpful but is not actually needed to make a diagnosis. Once a diagnosis of GBS is made, neurology should be consulted and he should start on IVIG or plasma
exchange as soon as possible to prevent respiratory failure and the need for mechanical ventilation. If the patient is not treated within an appropriate time, the patient will stop breathing due to respiratory muscle weakness.
‘Once the patient gets treatment for 3-7 days, the patient improves and can be discharged with followup.

48.caseSummary:
Differential: Community acquired pneumonia, Lung cancer, Lung abscess, Bronchitis, Pulmonary embolus, Legionella pneumonia, COPD exacerbation, and Bronchiectasis.

This patient has community acquired pneumonia caused by a streptococcus pneumoniae infection. This should be high on the differential due to the patient's worsening productive cough, shortness of breath, and fever. After
doing a physical exam (which reveals lung findings consistent with a consolidation), you should obtain basic labs, including blood cultures and a sputum sample for culture and gram stain, as well as a chest X-ray. The next
step is to determine if the patient is going to be treated as an outpatient or an inpatient. The table given is specific to give an idea of what to look for. It is not important to memorize this, but to get the idea that if an older
patient has an abnormal lab value or medical condition, itis likely that the patient will need to come into the hospital to be treated. In this instance, the patient has concerning vital signs (fever, tachycardia, hypoxemia), a low
sodium at 129 and is 64 years old (so, 64-10 (due to being female) = 54 + 20 = 74), so the patient should be admitted to the hospital and started on appropriate antibiotics. The patient should be treated empirically before
the culture results come back. Typical inpatient regimens for community-acquired pneumonia (without concern for MRSA or pseudomonas) include beta-lactam + a macrolide OR respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy
(ie. levofloxacin). After treatment for approximately one day, the patient will begin to feel better, and the patient can be discharged, and the case will end. The patient can be given the recommended vaccines to prevent

50.title: Headache
50.chiefComplaint: Severe unilateral orbital headache with lacrimation
50.caseSummary:
Differential: Intracranial neoplasm, Migraine (complicated), Partial seizure, Pseudotumor cerebri, Tension headache, Trigeminal neuralgia.

This patient has cluster headaches and has the classical symptoms of patients with cluster headaches which include: unilateral miosis, lacrimation, sweating, and severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital and/or temporal pain
lasting anywhere between 15-180 minutes. A CT or MRI should be done to exclude abnormalities of the brain and the pituitary gland, but the diagnosis of cluster headache is purely clinical so lab values and imaging findings
are usually not helpful. The treatment of choice is 100% oxygen which will make the patient feel mildly better. If this is not effective, the next abortive treatment is IM sumatriptan which should abort the headache within 20
minutes. The patient in this case does feel better and the case will end. The best preventive treatment for cluster headaches is verapamil, and this is first line treatment. Other modalities should only be investigated after
verapamil is determined to be ineffective.

Associated ipsilateral autonomic features: lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, eyelid edema, miosis/ptosis (Horner's). Patient is restless/agitated during attacks (unlike migraine where patient lies still). Triggers: alcohol during cluster period. More common in men. 51.title: Altered Mental Status
51.chiefComplaint: Transient focal neurological deficit, resolves within hours
51.caseSummary:
Differential: Migraine, Stroke, Hypoglycemia, Seizure, Subdural or epidural hematoma, Intracranial tumor.

This patient had a TIA which means that the patient has transient stroke-like neurologic symptoms that typically resolve within 30-60 minutes without evidence of acute infarction. The patient has risk factors for having a
stroke including diabetes, smoking, high cholesterol, and advancing age. In this case, the patient is unlikely to have any new or additional symptoms apart what was reported in the initial history, regardless of what you do.
However, the grading will be based on ordering the correct diagnostic tests and management of this patient. The patient should first get a head CT to rule out any hemorrhage. Then a brain MRI scan can be done for more
detail, as this test is most sensitive for identifying ischemic lesions. Both will be normal in this case, confirming the diagnosis of TIA. On exam, the patient has a bruit over his left carotid artery, so this should be evaluated
through a carotid duplex ultrasound, MRA or a CT angiogram. The stenosis is greater than 70% and the patient is symptomatic, so this patient should be scheduled for a carotid endarterectomy. Also, antiplatelet therapy
should be prescribed for this patient. There is debate about the best combination, but aspirin, or aspirin plus dipyridamole, or clopidogrel are good options. Once the patient is scheduled for a carotid endarterectomy, the

case will end. The patient should also be put on a statin, educated about his smoking and diabetes, and put on a diabetic diet.
51.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with transient focal neurological deficit (unilateral weakness, aphasia, visual field defect) resolving completely within 24 hours (typically <1 hour). Exam reveals carotid bruit on the right. TIA is a neurological emergency — 10-15% risk of stroke within 90 days, highest in first 48 hours. ABCD2 score predicts stroke risk. 52.title: Chest Pain
52.chiefComplaint: Chest pain at rest, ischemic ECG, negative troponin
52.caseSummary:
Differential: Aortic dissection, Costochondritis, GERD, ST-elevation MI, Non-ST elevation MI, Pericarditis, Pneumothorax, Pulmonary embolism.
This patient has unstable angina. This is a medical emergency and an acute MI should be immediately ruled out. This is done by getting an EKG which does not show any ST elevations, although it did show ST depressions

which could still indicate ischemia. Other life-threatening causes of chest pain, such as aortic dissection or pneumothorax, can be ruled out with a chest X-ray. Although initial troponin was negative, another troponin should

be drawn 1-3 hours later to assure a negative result. An echocardiography should be done to rule out structural causes of chest pain and heart failure.

Standard of care for treating acute coronary syndrome includes dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor), an anticoagulation agent (heparin, enoxaparin, fondaparinux, bivalirudin), a statin, and a beta-
blocker.Symptomatic management for unstable angina includes IV morphine and sublingual nitroglycerine for pain relief. Cardiology should be consulted, and the patient should be taken to the cardiac catheterization lab.
‘Once the patient is scheduled for catheterization, then the case will end. At the end of the case, itis important to counsel the patient about risk reduction for future cardiovascular events, which includes managing his
hypertension (for which he should be started on an ACE inhibitor or ARB), exercising, eating a healthy diet, and smoking cessation. If you would like, you can use the TIMI risk score for deciding about early invasive vs.
conservative management for non-ST elevation acute coronary syndrome. The patient has a score of 4, The patient has 3 risk factors for CAD (hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and smoking), is 65 years of age, presence of at
least 2 anginal episodes in previous 24 hours, and has ST segment deviation on EKG. Early angiography and revasculatization is recommended in these patients,

54.title: Yellow Baby
54.chiefComplaint: Jaundice in otherwise well-appearing term newborn
54.caseSummary:
Differential: Hereditary spherocytosis, Physiologic hyperbilirubinemia, Gilbert’s/Crigler-Najjar, breastmilk jaundice, hemolytic disease of the newborn/ABO incompatibility, biliary atresia, and G6PD deficiency.

The baby in this case has breastfeeding jaundice. Lactation (breastfeeding) failure causes jaundice due to inadequate intake of fluids and calories, causing slower bilirubin elimination and increased enterohepatic circulation of
bilirubin. The increased enterohepatic circulation also may result from reduced intestinal bacteria that convert bilirubin to non-resorbed metabolites. In this case, the mother's milk had not come in which led to a decrease in
milk intake which caused the patient's unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The first step in testing should be to determine whether this is indirect or direct hyperbilirubinemia. Once it is determined to be an indirect,
hyperbilirubinemia, hemolytic processes should be ruled out with a CBC (plus a smear and reticulocyte count) and a direct antiglobulin test for ABO compatibility (hemolytic disease of the newborn). Other causes of
unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia include hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, Gilbert's syndrome, and Crigler-Najjar. The baby’s total bilirubin was at a dangerously high level, which can lead to kernicterus and

permanent brain damage.

The baby requires hospital admission in order to receive phototherapy treatment to prevent permanent neurologic damage. While undergoing phototherapy, the patient's total bilirubin should be checked every 4-6 hours at
first, then every 6-12 hours once levels start falling. After 2 days, the patient's bilirubin has fallen outside dangerous levels, phototherapy can be stopped and the patient can be discharged with a followup in 7 days. While in
the hospital, the baby should be supplemented with formula until the mother's milk comes in, but the mother should continue to breastfeed the baby every 2 to 4 hours to help establish successful breastfeeding, Educating
the patient's mother about breastfeeding is important.

Review Later
54.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a term newborn presenting with jaundice appearing after day 3-5 of life, clinically well-appearing, feeding well, gaining weight appropriately. Breastfeeding jaundice is the most common cause of prolonged neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Pathophysiology: inadequate breastfeeding intake → decreased stooling → increased enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin. Must distinguish from pathologic causes: hemolysis (ABO/Rh incompatibility, G6PD deficiency), sepsis, biliary atresia (conjugated), hypothyroidism. Key labs: total and direct bilirubin (unconjugated > conjugated by definition), CBC with reticulocyte count (anemia? hemolysis?), direct Coombs (immune hemolysis), G6PD screen. Plot on Bhutani nomogram for phototherapy threshold. Management: optimize breastfeeding (increase frequency, lactation consultation). Phototherapy if bilirubin exceeds threshold for gestational age and risk factors. Exchange transfusion if signs of bilirubin encephalopathy or failed phototherapy.

56.title: Abdominal Pain
56.chiefComplaint: Acute abdominal pain, jaundice, dark urine
56.caseSummary:
Differential: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, DIC, Sickle cell anemia, Hereditary spherocytosis, Thalassemias, TTP, Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.

This patient has glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. The patient had a severe reaction to the oxidative effect of Primaquine, an anti-malarial agent. Ideally, G6PD deficiency would be tested prior to initiating
Primaquine, but the patient was treated in a local hospital in Africa which likely had limited resources to run this test. The patient presented with signs and symptoms consistent with an acute hemolytic anemia including
jaundice, fatigue, darkened urine, and abdominal pain. Lab findings showed a severe anemia (hemoglobin of 6.8 and hematocrit of 21) with other findings confirming an intravascular hemolytic process (indirect
hyperbilirubinemia, high LDH, high reticulocyte count, low haptoglobin, hemoglobinuria). Peripheral blood smear showing bite cells practically clinches the diagnosis of G6PD deficiency along with the history of taking
Primaquine. However, testing for G6PD deficiency during an acute hemolytic episode is not recommended, as it can yield falsely negative results, so this patient should be treated for the acute hemolytic anemia and then
followed up with testing ~3 months later and advised to avoid potential sources of oxidant injury. For this patient, treatment should involve immediately stopping Primaquine, resuscitating with IV fluids and packed RBCs in
the hospital, and treating the patient's pain appropriately. Once the patient is successfully treated, you can counsel him and his family about the diagnosis and to avoid certain foods/medications then discharge him home
with appropriate follow-up in 1-3 months, at which time testing for G6PD deficiency would be indicated,
56.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute abdominal/back pain, fatigue, jaundice, and dark urine (hemoglobinuria) following exposure to an oxidative stressor (fava beans, infection, certain drugs: sulfa, primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase). Labs show acute hemolytic anemia (low Hb, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, elevated reticulocyte count, indirect hyperbilirubinemia). Peripheral smear shows bite cells, blister cells, and Heinz bodies. G6PD deficiency is the most common enzymopathy worldwide — X-linked recessive. G6PD protects RBCs from oxidative stress. Trigger → oxidative damage → intravascular + extravascular hemolysis. Diagnosis: G6PD enzyme assay (do NOT check during acute hemolysis — reticulocytes have higher G6PD). Treatment: supportive — remove trigger, IV fluids, transfuse if severe anemia. Avoid oxidative drugs lifelong. Screen family members (X-linked).

57.title: Abdominal Pain
57.chiefComplaint: Colicky abdominal pain, currant jelly stools
57.caseSummary:
Differential: Metabolic disease, Enterocolitis, Small bowel obstruction, Volvulus, Incarcerated inguinal hernia, Appendicitis, Meckel's diverticulum, Gastroenteritis.

This patient has intussusception (likely ileo-colic, the most common type accounting for 90% of all cases) or telescoping of his intestines. This is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children between 6-36
months of age and is a medical emergency, as it can be fatal if not treated promptly. The patient has a classic presentation of intermittent abdominal pain, vorniting, bloody stool, lethargy, and a right-sided abdominal mass.
The patient should be admitted to the hospital and receive IV fluid resuscitation for his dehydration. Abdominal x-ray will demonstrate evidence of bowel obstruction with a R-sided mass (but without evidence of perforation),
and ultrasound will further characterize the mass as a classic radiographic “target sign’, further clinching the diagnosis of intussusception. An NG tube should be placed to help decompress the obstructed bowel and the
patient should be made NPO. Although pediatric surgery should be consulted and will follow the patient, first-line treatment for intussusception in a clinically stable patient without signs of perforation or shock is

nonoperative reduction via barium or air enema. In this case, nonoperative reduction is successful and the case will end at this time.
57.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a child (commonly 6 months - 3 years) presenting with acute severe colicky abdominal pain occurring in episodes, with drawing up of knees, and currant jelly stools (blood and mucus). Between episodes the child may appear normal. A sausage-shaped mass may be palpable in the RLQ (intussusception of terminal ileum into cecum — most common type). Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children <2 years. Peak incidence 6-12 months. Often preceded by viral illness (rotavirus, adenovirus). Diagnostic test of choice: abdominal ultrasound (target sign/doughnut sign on transverse view). Treatment: therapeutic air or contrast enema (reduces the intussusception in 80-90%). Do NOT attempt enema if perforation (free air on X-ray). Surgical reduction if enema fails or perforation present. NPO and NG tube for decompression. IV fluids for resuscitation.

58.title: Shortness of Breath
58.chiefComplaint: Barky cough, inspiratory stridor, respiratory distress
58.caseSummary:
Differential: Bacterial tracheitis, Diphtheria, Epiglottitis, Measles, Peritonsillar abscess, Retropharyngeal abscess, foreign body aspiration, anaphylaxis.

This patient has croup (laryngotracheitis) most likely from a respiratory virus. She has the classical findings of croup including a barking cough and respiratory stridor in the setting of recent upper respiratory symptoms (nasal
congestion) in the past 12-48 hours. Although croup can be diagnosed clinically with history and physical exam alone, a neck X-ray in this case would show subglottic narrowing and clinch the diagnosis. Because this patient
has stridor at rest and intercostal retractions, she should be sent to the emergency department for further management in case her respiratory status deteriorates. No further diagnostic testing needs to be done. In the ED the

patient should receive nebulized epinephrine, dexamethasone (either PO, IM, or IV whichever the patient can tolerate), antipyretics, and IV fluids. Once the patient is given the epinephrine and dexamethasone, the patient will
feel better and can be observed until the morning and discharged home.
58.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a child (6 months - 3 years) presenting with acute onset barky cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, and respiratory distress, worse at night. Often preceded by viral URI (parainfluenza virus type 1 most common). Croup is inflammation of the larynx and subglottic airway. Westley croup score assesses severity based on stridor, retractions, air entry, cyanosis, and level of consciousness. Classic CXR finding: steeple sign (subglottic narrowing on AP view). Treatment: mild (no stridor at rest) = supportive care, cool mist. Moderate to severe = dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PO/IM once ± nebulized racemic epinephrine. Dexamethasone reduces airway edema. Racemic epinephrine is for temporary relief only — observe 2-4 hours after administration for rebound. Hospitalize if requiring racemic epinephrine, stridor at rest, hypoxia, or dehydration. Avoid unnecessary agitation — keep child calm.

60.title: Abdominal Pain
60.chiefComplaint: Severe unilateral flank pain radiating to groin, hematuria
60.caseSummary:
Differential: Gastroenteritis, Pancreatitis, Perforated duodenal ulcer, Appendicitis, Ectopic pregnancy, Biliary colic, Ovarian torsion, Diverticulitis, Pyelonephritis

This patient has nephrolithiasis, commonly known as kidney stones. Her presentation of waxing and waning RUQ pain is very characteristic of nephrolithiasis and renal colic, plus her urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria, a
sensitive but non-specific finding. Although a CT scan is the preferred imaging modality for diagnosis, an abdominal X-ray (KUB) would also demonstrate a stone, as calcium oxalate (the most common type of stone
composition) is radio-opaque. It is important to rule out hydronephrosis from complete ureteral obstruction, as this would be an indication for a urology consult to intervene on the stone and either break it into pieces or
extract it manually. In this case, the patient does not have hydronephrosis or signs of urosepsis, so she can be managed conservatively with fluids, pain control, and an alpha-blocker (preferred) or calcium-channel blocker to.
facilitate stone passage. For pain control, opioids (morphine, hydromorphone) and NSAIDs (ibuprofen, ketorolac, indomethacin) are all appropriate options. The size of the kidney stone is also important to note; because the
patient's stone in this case is Smm, it will likely pass on its own without any further intervention. One study showed that 76% of patients with stones between 2-4mm passed them spontaneously without intervention. The

61.title: Headache
61.caseSummary:
Differential: Cluster headache, Intracranial neoplasm, Meningitis, Migraine headache, Pseudotumor cerebri, Sinusitis, Tension headache.

The purpose of this case is to have the user identify a benign condition and restrain from doing invasive, costly, or dangerous procedures. This patient has a simple tension headache, a very common condition that can be
diagnosed clinically and treated as an outpatient. The patient describes cardinal features including bilateral dullness, a “band-like” sensation and neck/shoulder muscle involvement which is supported by the physical exam
finding of pericranial and neck muscle tenderness. Otherwise, her exam and vital signs are normal. Importantly, she has no red flag symptoms that would necessitate brain imaging, such as “thunderclap” intensity and acute
onset, neurologic deficits, nausea/vomiting, or awakening from sleep. In her case, no further diagnostic testing is warranted before initiating treatment. The user would lose points if any invasive or costly test is done (such as
a head CT, MRI, or lumbar puncture). First-line treatments for tension headache include NSAIDs, aspirin, or acetaminophen. She should also be counseled about relaxation techniques, as stress is an exacerbating factor for
many patients. The patient will get better with simple NSAID therapy. Alternative treatments for tension headaches include caffeine, muscle relaxants, triptans and non-pharmacologic therapies such as physical therapy,
acupuncture, and trigger point injections. However, these are not first-line treatments and should only be used after the patient has failed first-line therapies.
61.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with bilateral, pressing/tightening (non-pulsating), mild to moderate intensity headache without nausea, vomiting, photophobia, or phonophobia. No aura. Not aggravated by routine physical activity. Duration 30 min to 7 days. Tension headache is the most common primary headache disorder — bilateral, band-like pressure. Distinguish from migraine (unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, nausea/photophobia, aggravated by activity) and cluster (unilateral with autonomic features). No imaging needed if history/neuro exam normal. Treatment: acute — NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) or acetaminophen. Avoid opioid and butalbital-containing analgesics (rebound headache risk). Prophylaxis if frequent: amitriptyline, nortriptyline (TCAs first-line). Non-pharmacologic: stress management, trigger avoidance, relaxation techniques, biofeedback.

62.title: Altered Mental Status
62.caseSummary:
Differential: Alcohol withdrawal, Cardioembolic stroke, Frontal lobe epilepsy, Migraine headache, Psychogenic, nonepileptic seizure, Syncope, Narcolepsy with cataplexy, Transient ischemic attack

The purpose of this case is for the user not to over-test or over-treat the patient in this case. This patient had a first episode, generalized tonic-clonic seizure. The roommate describes a classic presentation, timing, and
progression of a generalized tonic-clonic seizure with sudden loss of consciousness and muscle stiffening followed by all limbs jerking for a few minutes. After the seizure ends, the patient remains unconscious for a few more
minutes then gradually wakes up but is confused (part of a postictal state). Basic diagnostic workup of a first-time seizure in an adult includes chemistries and electrolytes (including blood glucose), magnesium, blood count,
urinalysis, toxicology screen, and EKG, although in most cases these will be normal like in this patient. Neuroimaging with a CT scan first is appropriate (especially since the patient fell from sitting so could be at risk for
intracranial hemorrhage) but then followed with MRI since this modality is more sensitive for structural lesions that could be responsible for seizure activity. This patient does NOT require treatment with anti-epileptic
medication. Starting anti-epileptic medication after a first-time, unprovoked seizure in an adult patient is only indicated if any of the following risk factors are present: EEG abnormalities, symptomatic cause based on history
‘or neuroimaging (.e. brain tumor or prior CNS infection), abnormal neurologic examination, or seizure that occurs during sleep. This patient does not meet any of these criteria, so he can be sent home with outpatient follow-
up in a few weeks. The patient should be counseled not to drive for several months, in case he has a subsequent seizure while driving.

Tongue laceration and urinary incontinence are common. First unprovoked seizure requires thorough workup: CT/MRI brain (structural lesion), EEG (epileptiform discharges, classify seizure type), labs (CBC, BMP, glucose, tox screen, LP if infection suspected). Alcohol withdrawal, electrolyte abnormalities (hypoNa, hypoMg, hypoCa), hypoglycemia, and CNS infection are common triggers. Do NOT start anti-epileptic drugs after single unprovoked seizure unless high risk (abnormal EEG, structural lesion, family history). Driving restrictions per state law. If recurrent seizures or high risk → start AED (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, valproic acid). Status epilepticus: >5 min of continuous seizure or recurrent without return to baseline = medical emergency (IV lorazepam/diazepam).

63.title: Malaise
63.chiefComplaint: Abdominal bloating, early satiety, weight loss, pelvic discomfort
63.caseSummary:
Differential: CHF, Liver cirrhosis, Leiomyoma, Other intra-abdominal malignancy.

The patient in this case has ovarian cancer. The purpose of this case is purely diagnostic and not meant to test your knowledge of ovarian cancer treatment. The patient presents with generalized symptoms (malaise,
unintentional weight loss) but after performing a complete physical exam and finding an adnexal mass, malignancy (specifically GYN related) should rise to the top of your differential, as this is a diagnosis you certainly do not
want to miss. Basic labs in addition to CA-125, a relatively sensitive tumor marker for ovarian cancer (elevated in ~80% of patients pre-treatment) should be obtained in addition to a pelvic ultrasound, the first-line imaging
modality for an adnexal mass, followed up by complete abdominal imaging (MRI or CT scan). Because the patient also presents with dyspnea, a chest x-ray would be appropriate and it shows a pleural effusion, again raising
your suspicion for malignancy. Based on all these findings, surgical exploration to obtain a tissue specimen is indicated, as ovarian cancer is a histologic diagnosis but staged surgically. It is important to realize here that the
standard-of-care method of biopsying an ovarian or fallopian tube tumor is through surgery (not image-guided). Once the patient's tumor is removed and sent off to pathology for evaluation, then the case will end,

We have received emails asking why you do not give platinum based chemotherapy and get a cancer diagnosis from pleural fluid and not do a laparotomy. The answer is that Epithelial, germ cell, and stromal cancers of the

ovary, fallopian tube, and peritoneum are staged surgically. Surgical cytoreduction is commonly in metastatic ovarian cancer which is done via laparotomy.

Definitive diagnosis: surgical exploration with staging laparotomy (TAH-BSO, omentectomy, lymph node sampling). Refer to gynecologic oncology. BRCA testing if family history (germline BRCA1/2 in ~15%).

64.title: Abdominal Pain
64.caseSummary:
Differential: Metabolic disease, Neurologic disease, Nonmetal intoxication, Other heavy metal toxicity, Epilepsy, Acute porphyria attack.

This patient has lead intoxication with encephalopathy; this is an emergency requiring prompt diagnosis and immediate chelation therapy! The patient presents with symptoms of lethargy, abdominal pain, vomiting, and
seizures in addition to a classic history of living in an older home undergoing renovation, which should raise your suspicion for lead poisoning. Basic labs (CBC, electrolytes, urinalysis, liver function tests) should be obtained in
addition to blood lead levels (which will show a blood lead level of 80 mcg/dl). The blood lead level in addition to findings of basophilic stippling on the peripheral smear will clinch the diagnosis of lead intoxication. Iron
studies should also be obtained as the patient also has a microcytic anemia; iron deficiency often exists alongside lead poisoning because risk factors for these conditions are similar. Finally, imaging studies including
abdominal x-rays (to look for ingestion of radio-opaque, lead-containing objects) and a head CT (to look for evidence of increased ICP) should be obtained in patients with symptomatic lead toxicity. The patient should be
admitted to the hospital, given IV fluids, lorazepam to control the seizures, and chelation therapy consisting of IV EDTA and IM Dimercaprol. The patient's symptoms will improve and his blood lead levels will fall over the
course of several days, at which point he will be safe to be discharged. It is important to counsel the family about the dangers of lead paint and attempt to involve social work or a lead abatement agency in assessing the
patient's home, as this was the most likely cause of the patient's elevated lead levels. Of course treatment of his acute lead intoxication is life-saving, but unless the home environment changes, he is at risk of future lead
intoxication.
64.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a child presenting with abdominal pain, constipation, irritability, lethargy, ataxia, and cognitive changes. History reveals exposure to lead-based paint in older home (built <1978). Lead intoxication causes microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling on peripheral smear. Elevated free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (FEP). Definitive diagnosis: blood lead level (BLL) >5 mcg/dL is elevated. >45 mcg/dL requires chelation. >70 mcg/dL is a medical emergency. Chronic lead exposure affects: nervous system (encephalopathy, developmental delay), kidneys (Fanconi syndrome), bone marrow (anemia), GI (colic). Treatment: remove source (lead abatement). Chelation therapy: succimer (DMSA) PO for BLL >45, or IV edetate calcium disodium (EDTA) + dimercaprol (BAL) for lead encephalopathy (BLL >70). Iron supplementation for anemia. Report to public health.

66.title: Cough
66.chiefComplaint: Chronic cough >3w, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss
66.caseSummary:
Differential: Fungal lung infection, Lung cancer, Lymphoma, Sarcoidosis, Vasculitis, Lung abscess.

This patient has pulmonary tuberculosis, likely a reactivation of a latent infection based on the location of cavitary lesions in the upper lobes. Suspicion for TB should be high due to the patient being from an endemic area
(Mexico) and having the classic triad of symptoms (fevers, night sweats, and cough). Initial workup includes basic labs and plain chest radiography, which will show upper lobe infiltrates. A CT scan will further demonstrate
cavitary lesions and hilar adenopathy, findings almost pathognomonic for pulmonary tuberculosis. Sputum AFB smear will essentially clinch the diagnosis, as it returns positive for acid-fast bacilli. Mycobacterium cultures
should be collected for drug sensitivity purposes, although these take several weeks to grow. In the meantime, the patient should be hospitalized, placed on respiratory airborne precautions, and started on the empiric 4-drug
regimen for TB: isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. It is important to obtain serum chemistries, liver function tests and hepatitis serologies (these were obtained anyway as part of STD screening) as well as a
baseline ophthalmologic exam prior to starting the medications, as isoniazid is hepatotoxic and ethambutol can cause ophthalmologic side effects. Vitamin B6 is also co-administered with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy. The
patient will begin to feel better after 3 days, at which time 3 negative sputum AFB smears should be negative before he is discharged. The patient should be counseled about the importance of medication adherence and
avoiding alcohol and other hepatotoxic substances. Finally, the case should be reported to the local health department so that appropriate contact tracing and testing can be performed.

Risk factors: immigration from endemic area, HIV, homelessness, incarceration, healthcare exposure. TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis — acid-fast bacillus. CXR: apical infiltrates, cavitary lesions (reactivation TB), hilar lymphadenopathy, Ghon complex (primary). Diagnosis: sputum AFB smear (rapid, less sensitive), NAAT (PCR), mycobacterial culture (gold standard, results in weeks). IGRA (QuantiFERON) or PPD for latent TB screening — positive in active and latent. Airborne isolation (negative pressure room, N95). Treatment: RIPE therapy — Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol for 2 months then INH + rifampin for 4 months. Directly observed therapy (DOT) preferred. Monitor LFTs (hepatotoxicity), vision (ethambutol → optic neuritis). Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) with INH to prevent neuropathy. Report to public health.

67.title: Frequency of Urination
67.chiefComplaint: Urinary frequency, urgency, nocturia, weak stream
67.caseSummary:
Differential: Bladder cancer, Bladder stones, Bladder trauma, Chronic pelvic pain, Cystitis, Neurogenic bladder, Prostate cancer, Prostatitis, Urethral strictures, UTI.

Performing an ultrasound can also help support the diagnosis of BPH and screen for suspicious lesions that could represent malignancy, although imaging is not necessary in the diagnosis of BPH. Another important test to
obtain is a post-void residual, either by performing an ultrasound of the bladder or measuring residual urine from a straight catheter after the patient has tried to completely empty his bladder. First-line treatment for BPH is
an alpha-1-blocker, such as tamsulosin, which typically provides immediate symptomatic improvement. An additional treatment is with a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor, such as finasteride, which acts through hormone signaling
pathways to reduce the size of the prostate. However, this class of medication takes 6-12 months to provide symptomatic relief, which is usually why monotherapy with an alpha-1-blocker is the preferred initial therapy. Once
medication management is prescribed, the patient will feel better and the case will end, It would be incorrect to immediately jump to a surgical operation such as a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) since this is
highly invasive, and the patient should fail medication management first before proceeding to a surgical procedure. Finally, it's important to counsel patients about lifestyle modifications to improve symptoms of BPH, which
includes limiting or avoiding alcohol and caffeine, as these are both mild diuretics.

68.title: Muscle Weakness
68.caseSummary:
Differential: Inclusion body myositis, Myopathy due to drugs/toxins, Myotonic dystrophy, Polymyositis, Polymyalgia theumatica, Hypothyroidism, Fibromyalgia.

This patient has myopathy secondary to statin use. Although generally considered safe medications, statins are known to cause different muscle-related adverse effects, ranging from mild myalgias to myopathy to severe
myonecrosis leading to clinical rhabdomyolysis. Combining certain medications, such as a fibrate (Gemfibrozil), with a statin further increases the risk of myopathy. This patient reports subacute onset of symmetric, proximal
muscle weakness and soreness within several weeks of initiating simvastatin and gemfibrozil and he has exam findings consistent with these symptoms (tenderness to palpation and lower extremity proximal muscle
weakness). Basic lab workup should include CBC, electrolytes, creatine phosphokinase (CK), inflammatory markers, TSH, Vitamin D level, and urinalysis. Results will show a moderately elevated CK, supporting the diagnosis of
myopathy, but normal urinalysis, which is important to rule out rhabdomyolysis-induced kidney damage. The patient's simvastatin and gemfibrozil should be immediately discontinued, and no further testing is warranted at
this time. The patient should also be encouraged to hydrate with lots of fluids to prevent kidney damage from myoglobin (a complication of rhabdomyolysis), although his urinalysis at this time does not show evidence of
this. If the patient's symptoms do not resolve after several weeks, further testing with EMG or muscle biopsy may be necessary to look for other pathologies causing his muscle symptoms. In this case, the patient's symptoms
resolve after a few days (sometimes it can take weeks) and CK levels are trending down. After the patient has adequate time to recover, it is reasonable to trial another statin alone (without gemfibrozil), particularly

pravastatin, fluvastatin, or rosuvastatin, since these have fewer reported drug interactions compared with other statins.
68.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive proximal muscle weakness, myalgias, and fatigue. History reveals concurrent use of simvastatin and gemfibrozil — a CONTRAINDICATED combination. Gemfibrozil inhibits CYP2C8 and OATP1B1, dramatically increasing simvastatin levels → myotoxicity. Labs show markedly elevated CK (often >10x ULN). UA shows myoglobinuria (risk of AKI). Differentiate from other causes: hypothyroidism, polymyositis, alcohol myopathy, steroid myopathy. Management: IMMEDIATELY discontinue simvastatin and gemfibrozil. Aggressive IV fluids to prevent pigment nephropathy from rhabdomyolysis. Monitor renal function and electrolytes (hyperkalemia risk from muscle breakdown). Alternative lipid management after recovery: atorvastatin or rosuvastatin (metabolized differently, less interaction risk), ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitor. Fenofibrate (not gemfibrozil) can be used with statins with caution.

69.title: Leg Pain
69.chiefComplaint: Unilateral leg pain, erythema, warmth, swelling, fever
69.caseSummary:
Differential: Calf tear or pull, Vasculitis, Deep venous thrombosis, lymphedema, Osteomyelitis, Popliteal (Baker's) cyst, Venous insufficiency, Necrotizing fasciitis, Toxic shock syndrome, Gas gangrene, Skin abscess, Erythema
migrans, Herpes zoster, Septic arthritis, Septic bursitis, Contact dermatitis, Insect bite,

This patient has cellulitis, which is an infection of the skin and soft tissues underlying the skin due to bacterial entry via breaches in the skin barrier. The patient is a diabetic, with poorly controlled blood glucose levels (as
evidenced by his elevated hemoglobin A1c), putting him at increased risk for bacterial infection. The patient initially presents with classic signs of infection, including fever and leukocytosis, and exam findings consistent with
cellulitis (well demarcated erythema, warmth, edema of the leg). Blood cultures should be drawn prior to starting empiric antibiotic therapy. The patient should also have a duplex ultrasound of the affected leg, to rule out
deep venous thrombosis as the cause of his leg pain, erythema, and edema. Empiric treatment options for cellulitis in a patient without risk factors for MRSA should cover methicillin-sensitive S. Aureus (MSSA) and beta-
hemolytic streptococci species. Because the patient has systemic signs of infection (fever and leukocytosis), inpatient treatment with IV antibiotics is warranted. In addition to empiric antibiotics, the patient should also be
given IV fluids and insulin to decrease his elevated blood glucose levels. After a couple of days with antibiotic therapy, the patient will get better and can be discharged home with oral antibiotics and insulin, with follow-up in

2 weeks.

69.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset unilateral leg pain, erythema, warmth, swelling, and fever. The affected area shows poorly demarcated erythema, warmth, and edema. Cellulitis is an infection of the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue — most commonly caused by beta-hemolytic Streptococci (Group A Strep) and S. aureus. Differentiate from erysipelas (more superficial, well-demarcated, raised borders). Risk factors: skin breaks, tinea pedis, lymphedema, venous stasis, diabetes, immunocompromise. IV antibiotics for severe/systemic symptoms (cefazolin, nafcillin, vancomycin if MRSA risk). Elevate affected limb. Treat underlying predisposing conditions.

71.title: Diarrhea
71.chiefComplaint: Chronic diarrhea, weight loss, bloating, fatigue
71.caseSummary:
Differential: linflammatory bowel disease, Lactose intolerance, Irritable bowel syndrome, Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, Giardiasis, Bacterial gastroenteritis, protein intolerance, viral gastroenteritis.

This patient has celiac disease. She presented with gastrointestinal symptoms including diarrhea, steatorrhea (foul-smelling, floating stools), bloating and weight loss, suggestive of a malabsorptive process. Her physical exam
is essentially normal (with the exception of skin findings consistent with dermatitis herpetiformis) and the majority of her diagnostic tests are negative. Current guidelines recommend anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA (along
with serum IgA levels) as the preferred first-line serology test, as it is the most sensitive and specific for Celiac disease, but as of now this test is not an available order on the USMLE exam. However, a positive anti-endomysial
antibody, as this patient has, is still highly specific for the diagnosis. The gold standard for diagnosis is a small bowel biopsy showing villous atrophy, which will clinch the diagnosis in this patient's case. Once the diagnosis is
confirmed, the patient should be put on a gluten-free diet, which will improve her symptoms. 70% of patients have noticeable clinical improvement within 2 weeks of initiating a gluten-free diet. In addition to nutritional

counseling and a gluten-free diet, the patient should be screened for vitamin and mineral deficiencies, as these can occur due to malabsorption. A bone density DEXA scan should also be obtained in all patients diagnosed
with Celiac disease to look for osteopenia/osteoporosis, a potential consequence of vitamin D deficiency. Finally, the patient should be given a pneumococcal vaccine because Celiac disease is associated with hyposplenism.

71.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, bloating, abdominal pain, weight loss, fatigue, and iron deficiency anemia. Celiac disease is an autoimmune enteropathy triggered by gluten in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DQ2/DQ8). Gliadin peptides are deamidated by tissue transglutaminase (tTG) → immune response → small intestinal villous atrophy. Classic extra-intestinal manifestations: dermatitis herpetiformis (pruritic vesicles on extensor surfaces), iron deficiency anemia, osteoporosis, peripheral neuropathy. Diagnosis: IgA anti-tTG antibody (first-line serology) + total IgA level (rule out IgA deficiency, which causes false-negative tTG). If IgA deficient, use IgG anti-tTG or anti-DGP. Confirm with duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytosis (gold standard). DO NOT start gluten-free diet before biopsy. Treatment: lifelong strict gluten-free diet. Monitor nutritional deficiencies (iron, B12, folate, vitamin D, calcium).

73.title: Memory Loss
73.caseSummary:
Differential: B12 deficiency, Chronic subdural hematoma, Depression, Hypothyroidism, Intracranial tumor, Neurosyphilis, Normal pressure hydrocephalus, Vascular dementia, Frontotemporal dementia, Dementia with Lewy
Bodies.

This patient most likely has Alzheimer’s dementia, a neurodegenerative disorder of unknown cause, and the most common cause of dementia. Key elements of this patient's history are the decline in memory (getting lost on
her way home) and executive functioning (difficulty paying bills), and her physical exam shows no focal neurologic deficits suggestive of alternative diagnoses that can cause neurocognitive dysfunction (such as chronic
subdural hematoma or normal pressure hydrocephalus). Mental status and neurocognitive assessment shows significant impairment in delayed recall of objects. Lab workup for reversible causes of dementia is unremarkable.
Although neuroimaging does not aid in the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease, it can rule out underlying structural brain lesions (MRI being more sensitive than CT), but in this patient's case the only finding is generalized brain
atrophy, which is usually age-related and fairly nonspecific. Treatment options for Alzheimer's dementia include cholinesterase inhibitors such a donepezil (most widely used, preferred first-line agent due to its once-daily
dosing and ease of use). Memantine is another treatment option, although it is usually only given in moderate to severe cases, as it has been shown to have little clinical benefit for mild cases. It's important to note that the
cholinesterase inhibitors are only for symptomatic improvement; they do not alter the disease course or slow progression of the disease. Memantine may be neuroprotective, although existing data is mixed on its effects on
disease progression. As always, it's important to give routine vaccinations and recommended screening tests for this patient.
73.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive episodic memory loss (recent > remote), difficulty with word finding, visuospatial deficits, apraxia, and decline in executive function, gradually worsening over months to years. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia. Pathophysiology: accumulation of extracellular beta-amyloid plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (hyperphosphorylated tau protein) → neuronal death. Rule out reversible causes: B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism (TSH), neurosyphilis (RPR), normal pressure hydrocephalus, depression (pseudodementia). Imaging: CT/MRI brain shows diffuse cortical atrophy (especially medial temporal/hippocampal). Diagnosis is clinical — supportive features. MMSE or MOCA for cognitive screening. Treatment: cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) for mild-mod AD. Memantine (NMDA antagonist) for mod-severe. Both provide modest symptomatic benefit — no disease-modifying therapy currently. Caregiver support, advance care planning, safety assessment.

74.title: Persistent Cough
74.caseSummary:
Differential: Lung abscess, Lymphoma, Sarcoidosis, Tuberculosis, Benign pulmonary nodule, Lung metastasis from unknown primary source.

This patient has lung cancer, specifically adenocarcinoma. This case is about initial evaluation and diagnostic workup as well as initial staging and management of a new lung cancer diagnosis. A new cough and hemoptysis in
@ patient with extensive smoking history should raise suspicion for lung malignancy. X-ray is the initial imaging study of choice, followed by CT scan for further characterization; in this case, CT features suggestive of
malignancy include large size (2.5m) and spiculations. Other lab studies and imaging tests are done to look for signs of metastatic disease or paraneoplastic syndromes (ex: SIADH or hypercalcemia). Bronchoscopy is

performed to retrieve a tissue biopsy of the mass (as well as mediastinal lymph nodes) needed for histologic diagnosis. Once the diagnosis of adenocarcinoma is made, surgery and oncology teams should be consulted for
further management. The patient should also be counseled about his new diagnosis and smoking cessation, in addition to receiving age-appropriate vaccinations and other recommended cancer screening tests.

75.title: Chest Pain
75.chiefComplaint: Severe tearing chest pain radiating to back, maximal at onset
75.caseSummary:
Differential: Pericardial tamponade, Myocardial infarction, Pericarditis, Pulmonary embolism, Esophageal rupture.

This patient has an ascending (type A) aortic dissection. This is a surgical emergency, and the case will test to see if you can make the diagnosis and get the patient immediately into emergency surgery. The patient's
symptoms of acute-onset, tearing chest pain radiating to the back in the setting of a history of hypertension in addition to exam findings of a new diastolic murmur (suggestive of aortic regurgitation) and systolic blood
pressure differential between right and left arms is highly concerning for ascending aortic dissection. The patient should be placed on a cardiac monitor, given supplemental oxygen and IV opioids for pain relief while an EKG
(to look for signs of ischemia) and chest x-ray are obtained. Initial imaging with a chest x-ray will show mediastinal widening, but definitive diagnosis requires either a transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE; preferred for
hemodynamically unstable patients or in those with signs/symptoms suggestive of ascending dissection) or a CT angiogram of the chest, which will show two distinct lumens within the aorta. Thoracic or cardiothoracic
surgery should be consulted immediately and the patient should then be given IV beta blockers (to lower heart rate and left ventricular velocity) followed by vasodilator therapy (to lower systemic blood pressure). Once
surgery has been consulted, the case will end.
75.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset severe tearing/ripping chest pain radiating to the back between the scapulae. Pain is maximal at onset (unlike MI which builds). Exam reveals differential BP between arms (>20mmHg), pulse deficit, new aortic regurgitation murmur. May have neurologic deficits if dissection involves carotid arteries. Risk factors: hypertension (most common), connective tissue disorders (Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos), bicuspid aortic valve, cocaine, pregnancy. CXR shows widened mediastinum (>8cm). CT angiography of chest/abdomen/pelvis is diagnostic. TEE can be done at bedside. Stanford type A (ascending aorta) = SURGICAL EMERGENCY. Stanford type B (descending aorta only) = medical management (BP control). Start IV beta-blocker (esmolol first — lowers dP/dt) then add vasodilator (nitroprusside or nicardipine). Target HR 60 and SBP 100-120. Consult cardiothoracic surgery immediately.

76.title: Fever and Rash
76.caseSummary:
Differential: Fifth disease, Measles, Meningitis, Rubella, Scarlet Fever, Drug allergy

This patient has Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum), most frequently caused by Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6). The classic presentation for Roseola is in infants 7-13 months old who develop high fevers for 3-5 days (can

often cause febrile seizures) that resolve abruptly, followed by the appearance of a macular rash on the neck and torso, spreading to the extremities. Infants are generally still well-appearing, active, and alert throughout the

course of the illness and treatment is mainly supportive (antipyretics for fever, ensuring adequate fluid intake, etc). The main point of this case is to recognize the clinical presentation and make the diagnosis without any

diagnostic tests and manage it conservatively without invasive measures.
76.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with fever, sore throat, and a diffuse erythematous sandpaper-like rash that blanches with pressure. Exam reveals strawberry tongue (initially white-coated then red), pharyngeal erythema with exudates, and Pastia lines (linear petechiae in skin folds). Caused by Group A Streptococcus pyogenes producing erythrogenic exotoxin. Diagnosis: rapid strep test or throat culture. Treatment: penicillin VK PO x 10 days or amoxicillin (first-line). If penicillin-allergic: cephalexin or clindamycin. Complete full course to prevent acute rheumatic fever (not PSGN — which occurs after skin infection). Children can return to school 24h after starting antibiotics.

77.title: Chest Pain
77.caseSummary:
Differential: Anxiety, Substance Abuse, Hyperthyroidism, Mitral valve prolapse, Panic attack.

This patient has new-onset atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. She is presenting because she is symptomatic, with chest pain, palpitations, and dizziness. The trick with this case is the patient's history of an
anxiety disorder and her recent stressors. However, as with all psychiatric disorders, a panic attack (which may present similarly) should be a diagnosis of exclusion and medical causes must be investigated and ruled out first.
In this case, the diagnosis is made relatively quickly with a 12-lead EKG. In addition to a history and physical exam, workup for new-onset atrial fibrillation in a hemodynamically stable patient includes 12-lead EKG, complete
blood count, serum electrolytes (especially for renal function, as this can preclude the patient from taking certain anticoagulants), tests to evaluate for predisposing causes (ex: TSH, as hyperthyroidism can trigger atrial
fibrillation), and chest x-ray. Echocardiogram should be done to evaluate for structural or valvular heart disease, but this doesn’t necessarily have to be done right away in stable patients, as results would likely not change
initial management decisions. Management in this patient includes rate control with a beta blocker (such as metoprolol) or calcium channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil) and then initiation of anticoagulation. The decision
to anticoagulate patients is based on the CHADS-VASC score. This patient scores a 3 (1 point for female sex, 1 point for age > 65, 1 point for hypertension history), so guidelines strongly recommend anticoagulation. After
receiving appropriate rate controlling medication, the patient's heart rate will decrease, her symptoms will improve, and she will spontaneously convert back to sinus rhythm (as most patients with new-onset atrial fibrillation
do within 48-72 hours). Cardioversion can be considered in a few weeks, but she will need to have been on appropriate anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks to minimize the risk of stroke periprocedurally.

In terms of choice of anticoagulation, updates to the USMLE now include DOACs (Direct Oral Anti-coagulants) including: apixaban, edoxaban, rivaroxaban, and dabigatran. These were previously unavailable. These are now
acceptable choices for anticoagulation. Coumadin is still considered gold-standard treatment for anticoagulating, At times outpatient Coumadin clinics may not be available, so an inpatient hospitalization may be warranted
to titrate up warfarin to an INR of 2.5, so both outpatient and inpatient locations would be acceptable for this case.

The question has been asked why this patient shouldn't be considered hemodynamically unstable and undergo cardioversion, Hemodynamic instability is typically defined as inadequate perfusion to vital organs. Having
severe tachycardia can lead to hemodynamic instability, but the patient is not there yet as the patient has a normal blood pressure. You typically start with rate control, and if the patient does not respond to rate control, then
you could consider cardioversion.

References regarding this topic:
AHA/ACC (2014, updated 2019): For AFib, hemodynamic instability (hypotension, shock, or acute heart failure due to rapid rate) warrants urgent cardioversion, Stable patients with AFib and rapid HR are managed with rate

control and evaluation of underlying causes (e.g, ischemia).

AHA/ACC Chest Pain Guidelines (2021): Chest pain with possible acute coronary syndrome requires rapid ECG, troponins, and anti-ischemic therapy. AFib complicating ischemia may necessitate rate control or cardioversion if

instability develops.

ESC (2020): Similar to AHA, recommends rate control for stable AFib with RVR and urgent cardioversion for instability.

78.title: Generalized Weakness
78.chiefComplaint: Generalized weakness, weight loss, flank pain, hematuria
78.caseSummary:
Differential: Colorectal cancer, Renal Abscess, Chronic kidney disease, Hypothyroidism, Malignancy of other origin.

This patient has renal cell carcinoma (RCC). He presents with non-specific symptoms including malaise, weight loss, and flank pain and lab studies show anemia, renal insufficiency, and hematuria, necessitating further work-
up with imaging studies. Although ultrasound may be an appropriate first-line imaging modality, CT of the abdomen/pelvis is the most sensitive imaging study for renal cell carcinoma, and will show imaging features
suggestive of malignancy (septations, irregular borders, and contrast enhancement). Surgery/urology should be consulted to remove the malignant tumor. In most cases, nephrectomy or partial nephrectomy is used to get

tissue for diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma prior to treatment. Partial or complete nephrectomy is first-line treatment for early stage RCC. Imaging studies of the brain and chest should be ordered to look for metastases. Once
Oncology/Urology/Surgery are consulted, the case will end.
78.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with generalized weakness, fatigue, weight loss, fever, and flank pain. Classic triad of RCC: flank pain + palpable flank mass + hematuria. However, triad present only in 10% — most present with incidental finding or paraneoplastic syndromes. RCC is an adenocarcinoma of the renal cortex, most common type: clear cell carcinoma. Paraneoplastic syndromes: hypercalcemia (PTHrP), polycythemia (EPO), hypertension (renin), Stauffer syndrome (hepatic dysfunction without liver mets). Diagnosis: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast — enhancing renal mass. Renal US differentiates solid vs cystic. No biopsy needed before surgery if resectable. Treatment: localized → partial or radical nephrectomy. Metastatic → systemic therapy (immunotherapy — checkpoint inhibitors, targeted therapy — VEGF/TKI inhibitors). Cytoreductive nephrectomy in select metastatic patients. Refer urology/oncology.
