79.title: Back Pain
79.caseSummary:
Differential: Urethritis, Structural urethral abnormalities, Acute pelvic inflammatory disease , Nephrolithiasis, Acute cervicitis, Acute cystitis, Ectopic pregnancy.

This patient has acute pyelonephritis, which by definition is considered a complicated urinary tract infection (a UTI that has extended beyond the bladder). The patient in this case is otherwise healthy and does not have other
conditions that would affect management (such as pregnancy or immunocompromised state). Acute pyelonephritis is suggested by fevers, chills, flank pain, costovertebral angle tendemess, and nausea or vomiting, with or
without the typical symptoms of cystitis. This patient has fevers/chills/flank pain. Outpatient management is acceptable for patients with mild to moderate illness who are not septic or have evidence of obstruction or renal
impairment who can be stabilized with rehydration (if needed) and antibiotics in an outpatient facility and discharged on oral antibiotics under close supervision. Inpatient management is warranted if the patient has sepsis,
evidence of urinary obstruction, severe pain, debility, inability to tolerate oral medications or oral hydration, pregnancy, or if there is concern the patient will be non-compliant with the medication. In this case, the patient can
be managed as an outpatient and inpatient admission is not necessarily warranted. Empiric treatment is with a fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin x 5-7 days) if there are no risk factors for multi-drug resistant
bacteria or contraindications to fluoroquinolone therapy. This patient's urine culture came back as susceptible to fluoroquinolones so she can continue with this regimen. Another acceptable option for outpatient therapy is
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Inpatient parenteral antibiotic options include ceftriaxone, gentamicin, ertapenem, or tobramycin. These broader spectrum IV antibiotics carry many risks, so it's important to start on first-line
treatment before switching to different agents. Use of nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin, and pivmecillinam should be avoided in the setting of pyelonephritis because they do not achieve adequate renal tissue levels. If these were
ordered, points would be lost.
79.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with fever, chills, unilateral flank pain/CVA tenderness, nausea, vomiting, and lower urinary tract symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency). Acute pyelonephritis is an ascending bacterial infection of the renal parenchyma — most commonly E. coli (80%). Risk factors: female, sexual activity, pregnancy, urinary tract obstruction, catheterization, DM, immunosuppression. UA shows pyuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, WBC casts. Urine culture for confirmation + sensitivities. Blood cultures if severe/septic. CT abdomen/pelvis if complicated (abscess, obstruction, stone) or not responding to 48-72h of antibiotics. Treatment: outpatient (mild, stable): PO fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) or TMP-SMX. Inpatient (severe, vomiting, pregnant, immunocompromised): IV ceftriaxone or fluoroquinolone. Switch to PO after clinical improvement. Total course 7-14 days. Repeat urine culture after treatment to confirm clearance.

80.title: Vomiting
80.caseSummary:
Differential: Duodenal web, Intestinal atresia, Intussusception, Meconium plug/ileus, Necrotizing enterocolitis.

This case is a case of malrotation of the gut with volvulus in a newborn infant. Malrotation occurs as a result of an arrest of normal rotation of the embryonic gut during organogenesis. Volvulus occurs when the small bowel
‘twists around itself, causing intestinal obstruction (responsible for patient's bilious vomiting, the most common presenting symptom) and potentially bowel ischemia and necrosis (due to the vascular supply being cut off and
why the patient's stool was red). The obstruction caused by volvulus can lead to severe dehydration and potential hemodynamic compromise. The important part of this case is to diagnose the problem quickly with
appropriate imaging studies (first with plain abdominal radiographs to rule out perforation then followed by either an upper Gl series or an abdominal ultrasound, either of which will show evidence of malrotation), consult

pediatric surgery once the diagnosis is made, and then treat the patient supportively with NG tube decompression and IV fluid resuscitation prior to surgery.
80.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a neonate/infant presenting with bilious (green) vomiting — a surgical emergency until proven otherwise. Bilious vomiting in a newborn = malrotation with volvulus. Malrotation occurs when the midgut fails to complete its normal 270° counterclockwise rotation during fetal development, resulting in a narrow mesenteric base. This predisposes to volvulus — twisting of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery → intestinal ischemia and necrosis. Diagnosis: upper GI series (gold standard) showing DJJ (duodenojejunal junction) to the RIGHT of midline and spiral/corkscrew duodenum. Abdominal X-ray may show double bubble sign or gasless abdomen. Treatment: EMERGENCY surgical exploration (Ladd procedure). NPO, NG tube decompression, IV fluids. Time-critical — delay leads to bowel necrosis and short gut syndrome.

81.title: Diarrhea
81.chiefComplaint: Chronic diarrhea, RLQ pain, weight loss
81.caseSummary:
Differential: Diverticulitis, Gastroenteritis, Infectious colitis, Irritable bowel syndrome, Ischemic colitis, Lactose intolerance, Pseudomembranous colitis, Small bowel lymphoma, Ulcerative colitis, Celiac disease, Small intestinal
bacterial overgrowth (SIBO).

This patient has Crohn's disease. He presented with typical symptoms including crampy abdominal pain and diarrhea and his labs indicated occult blood in the stool and elevated inflammatory markers. Diagnosis is made via
colonoscopy showing mucosal inflammation next to areas of normal mucosa (“skip lesions”) and linear ulcerations making a “cobblestone” appearance. These endoscopic features along with the characteristic involvement of
the terminal ileum and right colon with rectal sparing is indicative of Crohn's disease as opposed to Ulcerative Colitis. Once this is diagnosed, the patient should be started on budesonide or prednisone to improve symptoms
The use of 5-aminosalicylates such as mesalamine or sulfasalazine is less useful than it is in Ulcerative Colitis but can still be options for patients with limited ileitis and mild symptoms. Immunomodulators (azathioprine,
methotrexate, 6-MP) and anti-TNF agents (infliximab, adalimumab, certolizumab pegol (certolizumab is not yet available on the USMLE) are for higher risk patients with moderate to severe Crohn's disease but would still be
accepted in this case. Because the main focus of this case is diagnosing the patient and ordering appropriate diagnostic tests based on the history and physical exam, a wide range of treatment orders would still be accepted.

Consulting Gl is also indicated, as they will be the team helping with these complicated treatment decisions.
81.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic diarrhea (often non-bloody), RLQ abdominal pain, weight loss, fatigue, and fever. Crohn's disease is a transmural granulomatous inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus — most commonly terminal ileum. Skip lesions (areas of inflammation between normal mucosa), cobblestoning, creeping fat, strictures, and fistulas are characteristic. Extraintestinal manifestations: arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, PSC. Diagnosis: colonoscopy with terminal ileum intubation and biopsy (transmural inflammation, non-caseating granulomas). CT/MR enterography for small bowel evaluation. Labs: anemia, elevated CRP/ESR, fecal calprotectin. Treatment: mild-mod → budesonide (terminal ileal/right colon) or prednisone for induction. Maintenance: immunomodulators (azathioprine, MTX), biologics (anti-TNF — infliximab, adalimumab). Surgery for complications (strictures, fistulas, abscess) — NOT curative (disease recurs).

82.title: Abdominal Pain
82.caseSummary:
Differential: Giardiasis, Amebiasis, Viral gastroenteritis, Parasitic infection, Inflammatory bowel disease, Food poisoning (Salmonellosis), Hepatitis A, C. difficile infection, Cholera, Campylobacter infection, Shigellosis.

The patient has traveler's diarrhea from a bacterial infection (E. Coli, most likely enterotoxigenic strain) that he probably picked up from international travel to Central America. The patient can be started on an empiric
antibiotic (Azithromycin or a fluoroquinolone, such as ciprofloxacin) before the culture has returned and can remain on this since culture results demonstrated sensitivity to both options. An additional option to consider
would be an anti-motility agent, such as loperamide, which can help symptomatically but will not treat the underlying infection causing the diarrhea, so should definitely not be used as monotherapy.

Although most cases of traveler's diarrhea do not require antibiotic treatment and resolve within a few days, this patient has had severe (>6 stools/day), persistent diarrhea (>7 days) that is incapacitating and very much
interfering with normal planned activities. Other indications for antibiotic treatment (which this patient does NOT have) are fever and blood, pus, or mucus in the stool. In this case, the patient will continue to have diarrhea if
left untreated but will improve once antibiotics are initiated. It would also be important to counsel the patient about maintaining adequate hydration with fluids and electrolyte repletion.
82.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset nausea, vomiting, diffuse abdominal cramping, watery diarrhea, and low-grade fever. History reveals recent consumption of undercooked food or potential contaminated source. Most common causes: S. aureus (preformed toxin, 1-6h onset), B. cereus, C. perfringens, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella, E. coli. Most cases are self-limited (viral or toxin-mediated). Key: assess hydration status. Stool culture if: bloody diarrhea, severe illness, immunocompromised, >3 days, recent antibiotics or hospitalization. Treatment: supportive — oral rehydration (or IV fluids if severe). Antiemetics (ondansetron), loperamide if non-bloody diarrhea and no fever (avoid in dysentery — can prolong illness). Empiric antibiotics only for severe cases, bloody diarrhea, immunocompromised (fluoroquinolone or azithromycin).

84.title: Abdominal Pain
84.chiefComplaint: Acute LLQ pain, bloody diarrhea postprandially
84.caseSummary:
Differential: Adenocarcinoma of the colon, Crohn's disease, Diverticular bleed, Infectious colitis, Acute mesenteric ischemia, Peptic ulcer disease, Ulcerative colitis.

The patient in this case has acute colonic ischemia (also known as ischemic colitis). Intestinal ischemia occurs when there is inadequate blood supply to the intestines either from acute arterial occlusion, venous thrombosis or
hypoperfusion of the mesenteric vasculature. Colonic ischemia is the most common form of intestinal ischemia and 95% of cases are due to hypoperfusion, as seen in this case. The colon (particularly the left-sided colon or
“splenic flexure’) is most susceptible to hypoperfusion due to its limited collateral blood supply. This patient has risk factors for ischemia (age >60, history of hyperlipidemia) and became volume depleted due to a
gastrointestinal illness (note: work-up of the specific Gl illness is not the priority in this case!) as shown by his low blood pressure, tachycardia, and signs of acute kidney injury. His symptoms of crampy, severe, left-sided
abdominal pain and bloody stool in the setting of dehydration should raise suspicion for acute colonic ischemia. The patient should receive IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics and basic labs should be drawn
(chemistries, CBC, coagulation studies). An EKG should also be performed and his blood should be typed/screened in case a transfusion becomes necessary. Plain radiography of the abdomen will show pneumatosis (gas
within the intestinal wall) - a sign of advanced ischemia and CT will confirm the diagnosis of colonic ischemia. This case represents a surgical emergency and general surgery should be called right away. Once they are

consulted, the case will end.
84.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is an elderly patient with cardiovascular risk factors who presents with acute LLQ abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea following a meal (postprandial pain). Ischemic colitis is the most common form of GI ischemia — caused by non-occlusive hypoperfusion of the watershed areas (splenic flexure = Griffith's point, rectosigmoid = Sudeck's point). Differentiate from acute mesenteric ischemia (small bowel — embolic, more severe, pain out of proportion). CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast shows segmental colonic wall thickening, thumbprinting (submucosal edema/hemorrhage). Colonoscopy confirms with segmental erythema, ulceration. Most cases are self-limited and resolve with supportive care: bowel rest (NPO), IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics (cover gram-neg + anaerobes if severe). Surgery only if transmural infarction, perforation, peritonitis, or stricture.

85.title: Amenorrhea
85.chiefComplaint: Irregular periods, hirsutism, acne, difficulty conceiving
85.caseSummary:
Differential: Androgen-secreting tumor, Thyroid disease, Cushing's syndrome, Idiopathic hirsutism, Nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Ovarian neoplasm, Hyperprolactinemia.

This patient has polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Clinical suspicion for this diagnosis should be high based on the following: obesity, irregular menstrual cycles, features of hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne) and insulin
resistance (hyperpigmented skin in the axillae, also known as acanthosis nigricans). Based on the Rotterdam criteria (see below), she can be diagnosed with PCOS just based on her history and physical alone (oligomenorrhea
+ clinical signs of hyperandrogenism) although a pelvic ultrasound would demonstrate polycystic ovaries. Additional lab testing for workup of oligo- or amenorthea include a urine pregnancy test (beta-hCG), TSH, FSH, and
prolactin. A total testosterone level will also be elevated in this case. Because of the association between obesity, PCOS, and cardiovascular/metabolic disease, itis also appropriate to evaluate the patient for diabetes (fasting
or oral glucose tolerance test or hemoglobin A1c) and dyslipidemia (lipid panel). First-line treatment for PCOS in a patient not pursuing pregnancy is a combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive. This typically improves
both the clinical symptoms of hyperandrogenism and menstrual irregularities. An additional pharmacologic option to manage hyperandrogenism is an anti-androgen, such as spironolactone, but this is usually added after the
patient has already been started on a combined oral contraceptive.

Rotterdam criteria: 2 out of 3 of the following criteria are required to make the diagnosis:
Oligo- and/or anovulation

Clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism

Polycystic ovaries (by ultrasound)
85.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea, hirsutism, acne, obesity, and infertility. PCOS is the most common endocrine disorder in reproductive-age women. Rotterdam criteria (need 2 of 3): (1) oligo/anovulation, (2) clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, elevated free testosterone), (3) polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (≥12 follicles 2-9mm per ovary or ovarian volume >10mL). Other causes of hyperandrogenism must be ruled out: late-onset CAH (check 17-OH progesterone), androgen-secreting tumor (rapid virilization, very high testosterone), Cushing's, hyperprolactinemia. Labs: LH:FSH ratio >2:1 is classic but not diagnostic. Associated with insulin resistance → screen for diabetes (glucose, HbA1c, OGTT). Treatment: weight loss (first-line, improves all parameters), combined OCPs (regulate cycles, reduce hyperandrogenism), metformin (insulin sensitizer, improves ovulation), spironolactone (anti-androgen for hirsutism). Clomiphene or letrozole for ovulation induction if fertility desired.

86.title: Blood in Urine
86.chiefComplaint: Hematuria, flank pain, bilateral flank masses
86.caseSummary:
Differential: Renal Cystic Disease, Medullary Sponge Kidney, Von Hippel Lindau Disease, Renal cell carcinoma, Renal dysplasia, Simple renal cysts, Tuberous sclerosis, Wilms’ tumor.

The patient in this case has Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease. This disease usually presents with symptoms such as lower back/flank pain, hematuria, and hypertension. The diagnostic test of choice would be a
renal ultrasound, which would present renal cysts throughout both kidneys. Extrarenal manifestations include cyst development in the liver, pancreas, intracranial and coronary artery aneurysms. In the case, it is necessary to
lower the patient's blood pressure. ACE inhibitors are the first-line treatment for polycystic kidney disease as it is reno-protective and can protect from further renal decline. After initiating ACE inhibitors, the patient will begin
to feel better. Nephrology and urology should be consulted regarding management of the patient. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease increases the chances of having berry aneurysms. Not everyone with ADPKD
requires a MRA. Indications for an MRA would be: a family history of an intracranial aneurysm, patients about to undergo major surgery, patient working in high-risk occupations such as heavy machinery operators, patient
who require chronic anticoagulation. The patient does not know his family history, so it is reasonable to get an MRA in this case. The patient should be counseled to stop smoking, decrease alcohol consumption, and to avoid
contact sports.
86.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with hematuria, flank pain, hypertension, and palpable bilateral flank masses. Family history of ADPKD (autosomal dominant — 50% of children inherit). ADPKD is the most common inherited kidney disease — mutations in PKD1 (85%, chromosome 16) or PKD2 (15%, chromosome 4). Cysts develop in kidneys (and liver, pancreas) over decades, eventually causing renal failure by age 50-60. Diagnosis: renal ultrasound — multiple bilateral cysts in enlarged kidneys (usually by age 30 for PKD1). CT/MRI for more detail. Labs: elevated Cr (declining renal function), UA shows hematuria. Screen for cerebral aneurysms (berry aneurysms — 5-10% of ADPKD patients, higher if family history) with MRA/CTA brain. Management: BP control with ACEI/ARB (nephroprotective), treat UTIs aggressively, avoid contact sports (cyst rupture risk). Tolvaptan (vasopressin antagonist) slows cyst growth. Genetic counseling.

87.title: Abdominal Pain
87.chiefComplaint: Chronic bloody diarrhea, LLQ pain, tenesmus
87.caseSummary:
Differential: Crohn's disease, Diverticulitis, Gastroenteritis, Infectious colitis, Internal hemorrhoid, Irritable bowel syndrome, Ischemic colitis, Lactose intolerance, Pseudomembranous colitis, Ulcerative colitis.

This patient has ulcerative colitis. This is verified by a colonoscopy/sigmoidoscopy. Once this is diagnosed, the patient should be started on the first-line treatment which is mesalamine (a form of 5-ASA or 5-aminosalicylic
acid), or sulfasalazine (another form of 5-ASA). The patient will likely improve within 1 week, but may require 4-6 weeks or longer for clinical remission. There are other immunomodulators that can be used which would be
outside the scope of this test and would be used in cases refractory to mesalamine (5-ASA). It's important to know the first-line treatment, and you can consult a gastroenterologist if there is a need for a more complex
regimen.
87.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic bloody diarrhea, LLQ abdominal cramping, tenesmus, urgency, and weight loss. UC is an inflammatory bowel disease limited to the colon and rectum — inflammation is continuous from the rectum proximally (unlike Crohn's skip lesions), limited to mucosa/submucosa (unlike Crohn's transmural). Extraintestinal manifestations: PSC (most specific), arthritis (axial/peripheral), uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum. Diagnosis: colonoscopy with biopsy — continuous inflammation from rectum, friable mucosa, loss of haustra (lead pipe colon on barium enema), crypt abscesses, crypt distortion. Labs: anemia, elevated CRP/ESR, fecal calprotectin, p-ANCA positive. Severity determines treatment: mild → 5-ASA (mesalamine) topical or PO. Moderate → 5-ASA + steroids (prednisone or budesonide MMX). Severe → IV steroids, if refractory → biologics (anti-TNF — infliximab) or JAK inhibitor (tofacitinib). Fulminant/toxic megacolon → cyclosporine or colectomy. Increased colon cancer risk → surveillance colonoscopy starting 8 years after diagnosis.

This patient has signs of abuse. If the patient really fell into the bathtub with scalding hot water, then the patient would have burns all over his body, and not specifically in the buttocks, legs, and perineum. The scalding

90.title: Prenatal Followup
90.caseSummary:
Differential: Gestational Hypertension, Chronic hypertension, chronic renal disease, ITP, TTP, HUS, antiphospholipid syndrome.

The patient has pregnancy induced hypertension (PIH) (also known as gestational hypertension). PIH is defined as a new onset of hypertension (systolic > 140 and diastolic > 90) in the absence of proteinuria or new signs of
end-organ dysfunction. Severe PIH is defined as a systolic blood pressure > 160 or diastolic blood pressure > 110. This patient has severe PIH. The patient should be treated with antihypertensive medications until the baby
can be delivered. With severe PIH, the baby should be delivered at 34 weeks (2 weeks away in this case). The medications of choice are methyldopa, labetalol, or nifedipine. (Hydralazine is not recommended due to reflex
tachycardia). OB/GYN should be consulted as they will have to deliver the baby early. Magnesium Sulfate should also be administered for peripartum seizure prophylaxis in patients with severe PIH and for neuroprotection of
the fetus (even though she currently does not have pre-eclampsia). Once the antihypertensive agents are ordered, the case will end.

We have received emails stating that, according to the ACOG Bulletin 222 dated June 2020, pre-eclampsia with severe features can be diagnosed based on blood pressure alone. However, if you read the article, it lists the
diagnostic criteria for pre-eclampsia with severe features in Box 2, which DOES include proteinuria. Buried within the article, it then states that you can diagnose pre-eclampsia by blood pressure alone if systolic blood

pressure is > 160 or diastolic blood pressure is > 110.

In our opinion, this is intentionally contradictory information, as the authors do not wish to commit to changing the diagnostic criteria. This is still debated territory, and the USMLE typically does not involve material that is

still under debate. Therefore, for the purposes of the USMLE, we recommend using the traditional definition that pre-eclampsia requires proteinuria for a diagnosis.
90.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a pregnant woman >20 weeks gestation with elevated BP (>140/90 on two occasions at least 4 hours apart) and no proteinuria and no end-organ damage. This is gestational hypertension (PIH) — distinguished from pre-eclampsia by absence of proteinuria and end-organ dysfunction. Risk factors: nulliparity, advanced maternal age, obesity, family history, multiple gestation. Must monitor closely for progression to pre-eclampsia (up to 25% progress). Management: if BP >160/110 → antihypertensive treatment (labetalol, nifedipine ER, methyldopa). If BP 140-159/90-109 → conservative monitoring, no medication needed but close surveillance. ACEI/ARBs CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy. Serial monitoring: BP checks, UA for protein, fetal growth US, NST/BPP starting at 32 weeks. Delivery at 37 weeks (no later than term). If develops pre-eclampsia features → manage as pre-eclampsia. Low-dose aspirin 81mg for pre-eclampsia prevention in high-risk women (started at 12-28 weeks).

91.chiefComplaint: Firm, non-tender breast lump, possible skin changes
91.caseSummary:
Differential: Breast Abscess, Breast fibroadenoma, Breast cancer.

The patient in this case has breast cancer, specifically invasive lobular carcinoma. This is discovered first by doing imaging such as a mammogram or a breast ultrasound followed by a needle biopsy. Once the diagnosis is

made, consults should be made to oncology, general surgery for tumor removal, and radiation. Once the consults have been made, the case will end. This case will not test chemotherapy regimens.
91.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with a firm, non-tender, immobile breast lump with irregular borders, possible skin dimpling (peau d'orange), nipple retraction, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women. Most are invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC). Workup: diagnostic mammogram + breast ultrasound. If suspicious (BIRADS 4-5) → core needle biopsy for tissue diagnosis. Hormone receptor status: ER, PR, HER2/neu — guides treatment. Genetic testing: BRCA1/2 if family history, triple-negative, bilateral, or young age. Staging: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, bone scan, PET/CT if advanced. Treatment: surgery (lumpectomy + radiation vs mastectomy) + sentinel lymph node biopsy. Adjuvant therapy per receptor status: endocrine therapy (tamoxifen/AI) if ER+, HER2-directed therapy (trastuzumab) if HER2+, chemotherapy per Oncotype DX or stage.

93.title: Altered Mental Status
93.caseSummary:
Differential: Heroin/Opioid withdrawal, Stimulant (Cocaine, MDMA, amphetamine) or hallucinogen (PCP, MDMA) intoxication, Cardiogenic shock, Hypovolemic shock.

This patient has a Staph infection likely from “skin-popping” which can happen when heroin users who have a difficult time finding veins inject directly into the subcutaneous or intramuscular tissue. These patients are prone
to infections and abscesses. This patient likely tried to lance his abscesses which led to a systemic infection. The patient became septic and delirious which led him to be brought to the emergency department for further
evaluation. He is in septic shock and should first be admitted to the ICU. Supplemental oxygen, IV fluids and empirical antibiotics should be given. Blood and wound cultures should also be collected, although they should not
delay treatment. Acceptable empiric antibiotics should have MRSA and anaerobic coverage and include Vancomycin in combination with one of the following: a 3rd or 4th generation cephalosporin (eg, Ceftriaxone,
Cefotaxime, Cefepime), piperacillin-tazobactam, ticarcillin-clavulanate, meropenem or imipenem. It is important to consult surgery for recommendations to determine if debridement of the patient's wounds is necessary. It is
also important to contact social work and psychiatry to help to arrange treatment for the patient's current heroin use.
93.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with altered mental status, fever (or hypothermia), tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension unresponsive to fluid resuscitation — requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65. Lactate is elevated (>2 mmol/L) indicating tissue hypoperfusion. Sepsis = SIRS + infection. Septic shock = sepsis + persistent hypotension despite fluids + lactate >2. Source must be identified: blood cultures x2, urine culture, CXR, and cultures from any suspected site (sputum, wound, CSF). Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 HOUR of recognition — every hour delay increases mortality 7-8%. Initial resuscitation: 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid bolus. If still hypotensive → start vasopressors (norepinephrine first-line). Monitor lactate clearance (goal >20% decrease). Measure ScvO2. Admit to ICU. Source control: remove lines, drain abscess, debridement if needed.

94.title: Rash with Joint Pain
94.caseSummary:
Differential: Dermatomyositis, Drug reaction, Photosensitivity, Polymyositis.

This patient has systemic lupus erythematosus or SLE. She has a malar rash and joint pain which are classic signs of SLE. Other classic signs include fatigue, chest pain, mouth ulcers, skin lesions that worsen with sun exposure
(photosensitivity), and poor circulation in the fingers and toes. Her ANA and Anti-dsDNA are also positive. Many interventions can be done at this time, but itis first important to give steroids as the patient is in an acute
exacerbation. Also, it is important to consult nephrology (due to involvement of the kidney as evidenced by protein in her urine) as well as rheumatology. The patient's acute exacerbation will improve on steroid treatment
but may need additional therapy for management of her chronic disease. The patient should be counseled on her alcohol and tobacco usage. She should also be advised to use sun block.

95.chiefComplaint: Vaginal bleeding + cramping in early pregnancy
95.caseSummary:
Differential: Cervical or vaginal pathology (polyp, infection, neoplasia), Cervical polyp, Ectopic pregnancy, Menstrual period with dysmenorrhea, Spontaneous abortion
The patient in this case has had a spontaneous abortion, or miscarriage. Risk factors include prior spontaneous abortion and advanced maternal age (age 35 or older). Spontaneous abortion is diagnosed with pelvic
ultrasound and B-hCG and treated with expectant management, medication or a dilation & curettage (D&C) depending on severity of symptoms and ultrasound findings. This patient requires evacuation with a D&C due to.

her heavy bleeding. It is common to give prophylactic antibiotics like Doxycycline or metronidazole following a D&C to reduce infection risk. Methylergonovine will reduce bleeding and help to reduce the size of the uterus

Treatment: threatened → expectant management, pelvic rest. Inevitable/incomplete: expectant (allow to pass), medical (misoprostol), or surgical (D&C). 96.title: Nausea and Vomiting
96.caseSummary:
Differential: Meningococcemia, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, Toxic shock syndrome, Typhoid fever.

This patient has toxic shock syndrome due to her recent tampon use during menstruation. Toxic shock syndrome is a superinfection caused by S. Aureus, and recent tampon usage and surgery are the most common risk

infection, the tampon. It is also important to get blood and mucosal (vaginal) cultures and empirically treat the patient with broad-spectrum antibiotics, ie. clindamycin and vancomycin. In addition, this patient should receive
supportive measures such as IV fluids and oxygen. Patients not diagnosed and treated early are at risk of progressing into multiorgan failure.

97.title: Dyspareunia
97.caseSummary:
Differential: Hyperthyroidism, Hypothyroidism, Menopause, Pregnancy, Prolactinoma, Pheochromocytoma, Anxiety or Panic Disorder.

This patient is experiencing menopause. Hot flashes, a sudden heat sensation that is often generalized and associated with perspiration and occasionally palpitations, are the most common presenting symptom. The pain this
patient experiences during intercourse is due to vaginal dryness from decreased vaginal lubrication. All of these symptoms are due to decreased estrogen during menopause. Menopause is a clinical diagnosis, and does not
require confirmatory labs if patients are aged 45 years or older. Treatment options include: replacement estrogen with progesterone. There are risks inherit with this which include various cancers and blood clotting. Non-

hormonal pharmacotherapy includes SSRI/SNRIs (venlafaxine, paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram) or gabapentin. Risks and benefits of each treatment option should be discussed with the patient. Some patients may opt to
choose no intervention and, simply, wait out the symptoms which may improve with time.
97.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, hot flashes, night sweats, mood changes, and irregular menses/amenorrhea. FSH is elevated (>40), estradiol is low. Menopause = 12 months of amenorrhea. Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (atrophic vaginitis): thinning and drying of vaginal mucosa from estrogen loss → dyspareunia, pruritus, increased UTIs. Treatment: for vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes) — systemic HRT (estrogen ± progestin) for shortest duration at lowest dose. Contraindications: breast cancer, VTE, stroke. For GU symptoms only — vaginal estrogen (cream, ring, tablet). Non-hormonal: lubricants, moisturizers, SSRIs/SNRIs for hot flashes. Osteoporosis prevention: calcium, vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, screening DEXA.

98.title: Back Pain
98.chiefComplaint: Acute low back pain with sciatica
98.caseSummary:
Differential: Cauda equina syndrome, Compression fracture, Facet joint degenerative disease, Lumbar disk herniation, Spinal stenosis, Malignancy of the spine.

This patient's back pain and neurological complaints are due to lumbar disk herniation which has led to his back pain and

some neurological complaints. The treatment should be conservative. The patient should be started

‘ona short course of NSAIDs and encouraged to avoid physical maneuvers that may exacerbate the pain. The majority of patients improve within 1-2 weeks. Opiates are not recommended as first-line therapy and should only

be considered in patients who fail non-opioid management. No invasive treatment should be done at this time. Consider getting imaging if the patient has red flags like fever, weight loss, and bowel or bladder dysfunction.

These symptoms would be concerning for more life-threatening conditions like cauda equina syndrome or malignancy. It
acceptable to order these if serious neurological symptoms were observed.
98.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute low back pain radiating down the leg (sciatica) following lifting/twisting injury. Pain follows dermatomal distribution — most commonly L4-L5 or L5-S1. Exam: positive straight leg raise test (pain <70° elevation). Neurologic exam to identify affected root: L4 (patellar reflex, medial leg), L5 (foot drop, great toe dorsiflexion, dorsal foot), S1 (Achilles reflex, plantar flexion, lateral foot). Cauda equina RED FLAGS: bilateral sciatica, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention/incontinence, fecal incontinence — surgical emergency. Conservative management for uncomplicated herniation: NSAIDs, physical therapy, continue activity as tolerated (bed rest NOT recommended). Most resolve in 6 weeks. MRI if not improving or neurologic deficit (not urgent CT/bone scan — but MRI is gold standard). Epidural steroid injection for radicular pain. Surgery (microdiscectomy) if severe deficit, cauda equina, or failed 6+ weeks conservative.

99.title: Back Pain
99.chiefComplaint: Bilateral leg weakness, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention
99.caseSummary:
Differential: Compression fracture, Facet joint degenerative disease, Lumbar disk herniation, Spinal stenosis, Malignancy of the spine.

This patient has cauda equina syndrome. Cauda equina is caused by entrapment of the conus medullaris, the most distal portion of the spinal cord. It typically presents as low back pain that radiates down the leg with
perianal and perigenital numbness and/or loss of bowel and bladder function. Cauda equina syndrome is a medical emergency requiring prompt surgical intervention. Patients suspected of having cauda equina should
receive a STAT MRI and neurosurgery consult for spinal decompression. The key to this case is a fast diagnosis with a STAT MRI and a fast consult to neurosurgery. The case will end after neurosurgery sees the patient.
99.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with severe low back pain, bilateral leg weakness and numbness, saddle anesthesia (perineal numbness), urinary retention/incontinence, fecal incontinence, and decreased rectal tone. These are the RED FLAG symptoms of cauda equina syndrome — compression of the cauda equina nerve roots below the conus medullaris. This is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY. Delay in decompression leads to permanent paralysis, incontinence, and sexual dysfunction. Most common cause: massive central disc herniation. Other causes: trauma, tumor, abscess, hematoma. Diagnosis: EMERGENCY MRI of lumbar spine (do NOT wait). Post-void residual (PVR) >200mL supports diagnosis. Treatment: EMERGENCY neurosurgical decompression (laminectomy + discectomy) within 24-48 hours of symptom onset.

100.title: Vaginal Itching
100.caseSummary:
Differential: Atrophic vaginitis, Cervical cancer, Endometrial cancer, Vaginal cancer, Bacterial vaginosis, Candidal vaginitis, Cervicitis, Trichomonal vaginitis, Pelvic inflammatory disease.

The patient in this case has atrophic vaginitis. Atrophic vaginitis is an inflammation of the vagina (and the outer urinary tract). This commonly presents with vaginal dryness, discharge and postcoital bleeding in
postmenopausal women (due to the thinning and shrinking of the tissues as well as decreased lubrication). These symptoms are typically due to a lack of estrogen, which leads to the thinning and shrinking of vaginal tissue.
This patient should first get @ pap smear, a wet mount, and chlamydia/gonorthea testing to rule out gynecological malignancies and sexually transmitted infections. While nonhormonal moisturizers and lubricants can
address vaginal itchiness and pain with intercourse in mild atrophic vaginitis, they will not address this patient's vaginal discharge. Once malignancy and infection is ruled out, she should be started on a low-dose vaginal
estrogen. Vaginal estrogens (such as premarin) should be used with caution in patients with a history of breast or uterine cancer.In this case, once vaginal estrogen is prescribed, the patient will feel better, and the case will
end.

101.title: Fever
101.chiefComplaint: High fever, sore throat, drooling, stridor, tripod position
101.caseSummary:
Differential: Angioedema, Laryngotracheobronchitis (Croup), Caustic ingestion, Foreign body aspiration, Diphtheria, Laryngitis, Peritonsillar abscess, Retropharyngeal abscess.

This patient has epiglottitis, which is typically due to a Haemophilus influenzae type b infection. This is a medical emergency. In epiglottitis, rapid swelling of the epiglottis and surrounding tissues can lead to airway
compromise. Classic features of epiglottitis include difficulty breathing, drooling, and dysphagia. Increased stridor and “tripod” positioning, leaning forward with the neck hyperextended” are both signs of worsening airway
obstruction. This can lead to complete closure of the airway. Typically, the patient is transferred to an operating room while the patient is being intubated; however, this is not an option as there is no “operating room”

location on the test. This patient should be admitted to the ICU where he can be intubated and placed on a respirator if he decompensates. While the incidence of epiglottitis is low, rates are increasing due to the increased

prevalence of non-immunized children.

Diagnosis is confirmed when the epiglottis is observed during laryngoscopy for intubation. Imaging is not necessary to make the diagnosis. Once the airway is secured, blood and throat cultures can be collected. This patient
should be started on a 3rd generation cephalosporin (eg, ceftriaxone) and vancomycin to cover for the most common causes of epiglottitis: Haemophilus influenzae type b, Streptococcus pneumoniae (including strains that
may be penicillin-resistant), Group A Streptococcus, and Staphylococcus aureus (including community-acquired methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) strains). Because of this bacterial differential, empiric antibiotics should
also include an anti-staphylococcal agent such as vancomycin.

The classic lab diagnostic criteria for insulinoma is low blood glucose along with elevated plasma insulin, elevated C-peptide, and elevated proinsulin. Proinsulin is not yet on the USMLE, so this is not required. insulinoma is
very rare in real life, but it’s not rare on the USMLE as this is frequently seen on the test. This case is not how you would typically diagnose insulinoma. The gold standard diagnosis is 2 72 hour fast following by drawing
insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin labs. A 72-hour fasting order is not available on the USMLE, so this is not an option. Enough information is available to make the diagnosis without a 72 hour fasting test, but ordering a 72
hour fasting test is what would typically be done in real life. In this case, the patient has been fasting for 14 hours, so the lab data will be accurate enough to lead to imaging to look for an insulinoma, Abdominal ultrasound
or CT / MRI of the abdomen is appropriate. Contrast may or may not help in the CT/MRI, so either is acceptable.

The key in this case is to not be satisfied that the patient feels better after initially making the patient feel better by administering glucose. After appropriately diagnosing the patient, general surgery will need to be consulted
‘to remove the tumor.

If the patient is not a surgical candidate or refuses surgery, then Diazoxide, Octreotide, Verapamil, or Phenytoin can be administered. These medications can help prevent symptomatic hypoglycemia.

104.title: Back Pain
104.chiefComplaint: Localized lower back pain, fever, chills, malaise
104.caseSummary:
Differential diagnosis: Spinal tumor, Metastatic tumor, Spinal trauma, Spondylosis, Osteoporosis, Degenerative Disk Disease,

The patient has osteomyelitis to his lumbar spine. Osteomyelitis is an infection of the bone. It typically is a bacterial infection, but rarely can be a fungal infection. This patient has diabetes which is a risk factor predisposing
‘one to osteomyelitis. Other risk factors include: IV drug use, recent systemic infection (i.e. pneumonia, UT), immunodeficiency or immunosuppressive medications, obesity, malnutrition, trauma, and smoking. The most
‘common organism for causing osteomyelitis is Staphylococcus aureus (this occurs in over 50% of the cases). It is important to do a thorough neurological exam to look for neurological deficits caused by spinal cord

compression.
In this case, the patient has a fever, but fever is only present in about one third of patients with osteomyelitis. The patient also has an elevated WBC. An elevated WBC is only present in about 50% of the osteomyelitis cases.

Regarding imaging, MRI with gadolinium is the gold standard for diagnosis of osteomyelitis, but CT can also be used. A bone scan is not recommended to diagnose osteomyelitis because of its poor sensitivity. The MRI will
show disc space narrowing and disc destruction at L2/L3.

‘Once imaging confirms osteomyelitis, a blood culture and urine culture should be obtained prior to administering empiric antibiotics. It would be ideal to know the organism causing the osteomyelitis prior to administering
antibiotics, but the patient is already having disc space narrowing and disc destruction, so empiric antibiotics should be given. Empiric antibiotics should be vancomycin plus one of the following: ceftazidime, cefotaxime,

ceftriaxone, cefepime, or ciprofloxacin.

The patient should be transferred to the inpatient unit for IV antibiotics. The patient will require 6 weeks of antibiotic treatment. The case will end after 3 days of successful antibiotic treatment.
104.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with localized lower back pain, fever, chills, malaise, and point tenderness over the affected vertebrae. Vertebral osteomyelitis is a bacterial infection of the vertebral body — most commonly S. aureus. Risk factors: IV drug use, recent bacteremia, indwelling catheters, DM, immunocompromised. Diagnosis: MRI spine with contrast (gold standard — high sensitivity). Plain X-ray may be normal early (need 30-50% bone loss to see). Blood cultures x2 (positive in 50%). If blood cultures negative → CT-guided or open biopsy for culture. ESR and CRP elevated. Treatment: IV antibiotics (empiric: vancomycin + ceftriaxone or cefepime — cover MRSA and gram-negatives) x 6 weeks minimum, tailored to culture results. Surgical debridement if abscess, neurologic deficit, spinal instability, or failure of medical therapy.

105.title: Abdominal Pain
105.chiefComplaint: Acute severe pelvic pain, possible vaginal bleeding
105.caseSummary:
Differential diagnosis: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy, Endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, Adnexal torsion, Appendicitis

The patient has a ruptured ovarian cyst. Ovarian cysts occur commonly in menstruating women aged 18-35 years and are commonly identified by ultrasound. Two types of functional ovarian cysts are follicular cysts and
corpus luteum cysts.

While most hemorrhage associated with ovarian cysts have an unclear etiology, there are some risk factors which include: anticoagulation therapy and abdominal trauma. The right ovary tends to rupture more often than the
left ovary.

Typically at the time of rupture, there may be sharp and sudden onset of pain, which typically does not have typical characteristics. Blood loss can vary from very little bleeding to hypovolemic shock as is in this case.

Ultrasonic evidence of large amounts of peritoneal fluid and severe pain is an indication for operative intervention as well as decreased hematocrit and unstable vital signs. The patient in this case required surgical

intervention although most patients only require observation and some analgesics.

There is no preventive treatment in this case.
105.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset severe unilateral pelvic/abdominal pain following activity (intercourse, exercise). May have vaginal bleeding. Exam reveals peritoneal signs, adnexal tenderness, possible palpable mass. Ruptured ovarian cyst → bleeding into peritoneal cavity → hemoperitoneum → hypovolemia and acute abdomen. Most common: ruptured corpus luteum cyst. Differential: ectopic pregnancy (MUST rule out — HCG), PID, appendicitis, ovarian torsion. Diagnosis: HCG negative (rules out ectopic). Transvaginal ultrasound shows free fluid in pelvis/abdomen, ruptured cyst, possible adnexal mass. CBC for anemia from blood loss. Type and screen. Management: stable → observation, analgesia, serial hematocrit. Unstable/hypotensive → IV fluids, blood transfusion if needed, surgical consult (laparoscopy vs laparotomy for hemostasis). If on anticoagulation → reverse.

106.title: Fatigue
106.caseSummary:
Differential diagnosis: Transfusion reaction, Chemotherapy, Tumor related fever, Tumor lysis syndrome.

The patient is severely neutropenic. He has an ANC of 475 (calculated by taking 2500 and times by Bands + Segmented neutrophils (17% + 2%) = 2500 * 19% = 475). Severe neutropenia is an ANC < 500. The patient is at
severe risk and should be admitted immediately and started on empiric antibiotics. In a neutropenic patient, antibiotics should be administered within 60 minutes of presentation (some say as early as 30 minutes within
presentation). Experts have compared a neutropenic patient to be as serious as a myocardial infarction patient which requires swift and immediate treatment. The goal of this case is to teach how to quickly diagnose the

patient with severe neutropenia and then quickly administer antibiotics.

The source of the infection in this case will not be known. Only 20-30% of patients with chemotherapy induced neutropenia will have a known source of infection. In the other 70-80% of the cases, the presumption is that the
source of infection comes from the bacterial flora of the intestines. Although the case will end before the bacterial cultures will return, the culture would have been positive for Psuedomonas aeruginosa, so antipseudomonal
antibiotics will be required in the case. The antibiotic treatment recommended by the IDSA for empiric treatment for a neutropenic patient is monotherapy with one of the following antibiotics: Cefepime, Meropenem,
Imipenem, Piperacillin-tazobactam, or Ceftazidime. These have activity against Psuedomonas aeruginosa which in this case is the bacterial agent responsible for the patient's initial presentation.
106.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with fever (single temp >38.3°C or sustained >38.0°C for 1h) and absolute neutrophil count <500 cells/µL. This is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY — mortality high without immediate antibiotics. Most commonly seen post-chemotherapy. Often no localizing signs of infection because there are no neutrophils to create pus/inflammation. Blood cultures x2, UA + culture, CXR. Calculate MASCC score for risk stratification (low-risk may be outpatient). Treatment: empiric IV antibiotics within 1 HOUR — monotherapy with anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime, meropenem, pip-tazo). Add vancomycin if: hemodynamic instability, suspected catheter infection, skin/soft tissue infection, known MRSA colonization, severe mucositis. If persists >4-7 days → add antifungal coverage. G-CSF may be considered. Admit. Reverse isolation (neutropenic precautions).

107.title: Paranoia
107.caseSummary:
Differential diagnosis: Substance induced psychotic disorder, Schizoaffective disorder, Psychosis secondary to a medical condition, Major depressive disorder with psychotic features, Bipolar disorder, Delusional disorder,
Schizophreniform disorder.

The patient meets DSM-5 criteria for schizophrenia, The patient has both delusions (thinking aliens possessed his neighbor. This is a bizarre delusion) and hallucinations (hearing voices telling him that his neighbor is
dangerous). These symptoms are obviously impairing his life and has been going on for over 6 months which was obtained through collateral information from his mother. There was no history of a mood disorder such as
mania or depression. The patient did admit to using marijuana which was also positive on his urine drug screen, but the severity of the symptoms and the duration would make Schizophrenia the more appropriate diagnosis.
The patient also is in the standard age group where patients who develop Schizophrenia typically will manifest symptoms (which is in their late teens to early 20s). College is a common time where patients will manifest their
first episode of psychosis as it can be a stressful time away from support systems.

The most common treatments in an inpatient psychiatric setting or an emergency room setting with an uncooperative patient would be to offer oral medication, and if the patient refuses, then you would give IM
antipsychotics. This is typically IM Haldol, IM Olanzapine (Zyprexa), IM Aripiprazole (Abilify), or IM Ziprasidone (Geodon). Haldol is the most commonly administered in hospital emergency settings due to availability. If the
patient is willing to take oral, then oral Olanzapine (Zyprexa Zydis) is very popular because it is a dissolvable wafer that is very fast acting. If Haldol is given, this is typically administered with Lorazepam (Ativan) along with
Cogentin or Benadryl to avoid a potential EPS (Extrapyramidal Syndrome) including dystonias. This can be given while using IM second generation antipsychotics, but not necessary. A typical regimen given is colloquially
called the 5-2-1 meaning 5mg of IM Haldol, 2mg of IM Ativan, and Img of IM Cogentin. As Cogentin IM is very expensive, an alternative is a 5-2-50 which is 5mg of IM Haldol, 2mg of IM Ativan, and 50mg of IM Benadryl
(Diphenhydramine).

It is important to note that it is contraindicated to administer IM benzodiazepines when using IM Olanzapine (Zyprexa) due to the risk for fatal respiratory depression.

There has been a lot of debate on if itis better to start a patient on a first generation or second-generation antipsychotic. The answer is nuanced and above the scope of the test, but essentially, they both are effective in
treating psychosis, but you are choosing side effect profiles. First generation antipsychotics such as Haldol have a higher risk for akathisia, EPS, and tardive dyskinesia while second generation antipsychotics have a higher risk
for metabolic issues such as weight gain, diabetes, and cholesterol problems. In reality, most patients are initially treated emergently with IM Haldol and then transitioned to a second-generation antipsychotic. Tardive
dyskinesia can be a permanent condition and is a favorite source of litigation for lawyers. It is much harder to prove that a patient gained weight, became diabetic, and had cholesterol issues which can be directly tied to the
medication. Schizophrenia patients tend to not have healthy diets due to lack of access to fresh fruits/vegetables due to socioeconomic forces. The argument can be made that their diet has caused their metabolic issues. On
the USMLE, either first generation or second generation will be accepted as an acceptable treatment for schizophrenia. There are quite a few antipsychotics to choose from, and no antipsychotic has been proven to be more

effective than one another (except clozapine but see above as to why this is incorrect to use for a first episode psychotic patient).
In the real world, once the patient has become cooperative, it is important to get a baseline AIMS to monitor the medication in case the patient starts to develop abnormal muscular movements associated with tardive

dyskinesia, The AIMS test is not an order on the USMLE right now(surprise, surprise), but be aware that this is standard of care.
107.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with paranoia, auditory hallucinations (hearing voices), disorganized speech/behavior, negative symptoms (flat affect, social withdrawal, avolition), and functional decline >6 months. Schizophrenia is a chronic psychiatric disorder — symptoms for ≥6 months with ≥1 month of active symptoms. Must rule out substance-induced psychosis, medical causes (CNS tumor, infection, autoimmune encephalitis, thyroid), and other psychiatric disorders (bipolar with psychosis, schizoaffective). Diagnosis is clinical — no diagnostic test. Collateral history crucial. Treatment: antipsychotics (second-generation: risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole — fewer EPS than first-gen like haloperidol). Clozapine for treatment-resistant. Monitor for metabolic syndrome (weight, glucose, lipids). Long-acting injectables for non-adherence. Psychosocial interventions: CBT, family therapy, supported employment. Safety assessment for self-harm/aggression.

109.title: Unresponsive
109.caseSummary:
Differential diagnosis: Hypoglycemia, Alcohol intoxication, Opioid overdose, Other intoxicant.

The patient overdosed on diazepam which is a benzodiazepine with a long half-life. As benzodiazepines are commonly prescribed around the world, it is common that benzodiazepines are involved in overdose attempts. This
case is about restraining from too much intervention. The vitals of the patient in this case were within normal limits. The patient does not need to be intubated. Activated charcoal should be avoided as it provides no benefit
in benzodiazepine overdose and increases the risk of aspiration. Flumazenil administration in benzodiazepine overdose is controversial. Administering Flumazenil can cause withdrawal seizures, so this is an optional order. The
patient overdosed on Diazepam which has a long half-life, so if vitals are stable, it is unlikely that the patient will develop withdrawal seizures. No antiseizure medication is necessary.

The patient only requires supportive care in this case. IV fluids, a psychiatry consult, and time are the treatment for this patient. After enough time has passed, the patient will awaken, and the case will end.

110.title: Rash
110.chiefComplaint: Diffuse rash involving palms and soles
110.caseSummary:
Differential: Measles, HIV, Chlamydia, Gonorrhea, HSV, Rocky Mountain Spotted fever

The patient has secondary syphilis. From the history of present illness, the patient had a single painless chancre on his penis 6 weeks ago which resolved without treatment. This stage of a painless chancre at the site of
infection is called primary syphilis. Secondary syphilis which can last weeks to months. It can then go latent and become asymptomatic for years. It can then develop into tertiary syphilis which can involve multisystemic
systems including cardiovascular system, bones, neurosyphilis, and many other systems which can mimic many diseases. Syphilis is colloquially known as the great imitator.

The patient is currently experiencing common symptoms of secondary syphilis which can include: rash (disseminated or rash involving soles/palms as in this case), malaise, alopecia, fever, pharyngitis. Syphilis cases have
begun to increase again in the United States. It was previously on decline until 2000. Syphilis in men has been increasing primarily in the cohort of men who have sex with men. Methamphetamine use and frequent new sexual
encounters are risk factors for Syphilis.

HIV is a common coinfection for those with Syphilis, so this should be tested. Other sexually transmitted infections such chlamydia, gonorrhea, Hep A/B/C should be tested in this case.

Testing for Syphilis is done by performing both a nontreponemal test (RPR, VDRL, TRUST(not a current order on the USMLE)) and a treponemal test(FTA-ABS, MHA-TP, TPPA(not currently an order), TP-ElA(not a currently an
order), or ClA(not a currently an order)).

Typically, once a nontreponemal test such as a RPR or a VDRL is positive, then a confirmatory treponemal test will be done such as an FTA-ABS or an MHA-TP. The limitation of an FTA-ABS is that once it is positive, it will be
positive for life, so a previous infection could have made it positive. Although not done much anymore, a Darkfield Microscopy can be done which is definitive evidence of a Syphilis infection. For the USMLE to simplify, you
should simply get an RPR/VORL first, and if positive, get an FTA-ABS, MHA-TP, or a darkfield exam to confirm.

The patient should be treated with Penicillin G benzathine (2.4 million units IM x 1 dose). Other options in case the patient is allergic or had adverse reactions to penicillin would be: Doxycycline, Ceftriaxone, Tetracycline or
Amoxicillin. The patient's symptoms should resolve after treatment over the next 24-36 hours. The patient should be screened at 6- and 12-months following treatment to assure that the patient has become nonreactive to
syphilis screening tests.
110.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with rash, lymphadenopathy, and possible genital lesion history. Secondary syphilis: diffuse maculopapular rash (INCLUDING palms and soles — key differentiating feature), condyloma lata (wart-like lesions in moist areas), lymphadenopathy, flu-like symptoms. Primary syphilis: painless indurated chancre at inoculation site (resolves spontaneously). Caused by Treponema pallidum (spirochete). Diagnosis: screening with RPR or VDRL (non-treponemal — titer correlates with disease activity). Confirm with treponemal-specific test (FTA-ABS, TP-PA). Darkfield microscopy of chancre fluid can directly visualize spirochetes. HIV testing (high co-infection). Treatment: benzathine penicillin G 2.4M units IM once (primary/secondary/early latent). Doxycycline if penicillin-allergic. Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction may occur (fever, myalgias, headache within 24h). Report to public health. Partner notification. Follow RPR titers to confirm cure (4-fold decline).

111.title: Shortness of Breath
111.chiefComplaint: Acute dyspnea, petechial rash post long bone fracture
111.caseSummary:
Differential: Pulmonary Embolism, Air embolism, Aspiration, Heart failure, Pneumonia, Systemic lupus erythematosus.

The patient has fat embolism syndrome (FES). This typically occurs from hours to days to weeks after an initial injury that allows fat globules (typically from bone marrow) to enter the blood stream. Long bones such as a
femur are common causes of FES. FES, as in this case, can cause respiratory distress, and if intervention is not done quickly, then death soon will follow.

The patient has many metabolic abnormalities. He has both anemia and thrombocytopenia which are very common in fat embolism syndrome. He also has metabolic acidosis, increased level of BUN, and increased creatinine

which are also commonly seen in fat embolism syndrome.

Diagnosis is mainly clinical as imaging is not very reliable. Chest x-rays and CT scans can be normal as in this case. The patient would have an abnormal VQ scan, but this will take too much time to administer. The patient will
require immediate supportive treatment.

A commonly used criteria is the Gurd and Wilsons criteria for fat embolism to help clinicians determine if the patient is suffering from a fat embolism. The major criteria are:
Axillary or subconjunctival petechiae

Hypoxemia PaO2 <60 mm Hg

Central nervous system depression disproportionate to hypoxemia

Pulmonary edema

There are minor criteria, but these will not be listed. The pertinent positives in the minor criteria are Tachycardia more than 110 beats per minute, and fat globules present in the urine, At least two positive major criteria plus
‘one minor criteria is suggestive of fat embolism. In this case, the patient has axillary petechiae, hypoxemia, and tachycardia. Fat globules in the urine is not a current order on the USMLE.

Treatment is supportive. The patient should be transferred to the ICU, intubated, and put on a ventilator. The patient should be given fluids. Albumin therapy is considered experimental and corticosteroids administration is
controversial, so the mainstay treatment is just supportive. One thing to avoid is heparin/anticoagulant treatment. This has not shown benefit in fat embolism cases, and this increases the risk of hemorrhage.

Review Later
111.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia, petechial rash (chest, axillae, conjunctivae), and CNS changes (confusion, AMS) 24-72 hours after a long bone fracture (femur, tibia) or pelvic fracture. Fat embolism syndrome is caused by fat globules from bone marrow entering venous circulation → lodged in pulmonary and cerebral capillaries → mechanical obstruction + inflammatory cascade. Triad: respiratory distress + petechial rash + CNS dysfunction. Diagnosis is clinical (no gold standard test). CXR may show diffuse bilateral infiltrates (ARDS pattern). ABG: hypoxemia, A-a gradient elevated. UA may show fat globules in urine. Treatment: SUPPORTIVE — oxygen, respiratory support (may require mechanical ventilation). Early surgical fixation of long bone fractures reduces risk. Maintain adequate oxygenation and hemodynamics.

112.title: Found Unconscious
112.chiefComplaint: Found unconscious with signs of physical assault
112.caseSummary:
Differential: Alcohol intoxication, Syncopal episode, Hypoglycemia

This case is deceptively more involved than it first appears. There are a lot of factors to consider in this case. First, a rape-kit should be done to get forensic evidence that will be needed. It appears that the patient knows the
suspect of the rape. The patient has the semen of the perpetrator in her vagina, and this will be collected as evidence for prosecution.

The patient should then have a pregnancy test done to assure that she was not pregnant prior to this event as she will be given postcoital contraception (Ulipristal Acetate or Levonorgestrel). Once the pregnancy test is
negative, the patient should be given contraception (Ulipristal Acetate or Levonorgestrel). Then empiric antibiotics should be given for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomoniasis. This included ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and

metronidazole (or tinidazole).

The patient should then have psychiatry/psychology involved to follow-up with the patient to process the trauma that she has experienced. Social services should be involved to help with the facilitation of law enforcement
involvement, evidence collection, and follow-up.

The patient should be tested for Syphilis, Gonorrhea, HIV, Chlamydia, at 1 month after exposure and then again at 3 months after exposure. The patient should be counseled to abstain from intercourse until prophylactic

treatment is completed and condom use until serologic testing is completed. She should also be given a HPV vaccine.
112.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents found unconscious with signs of physical struggle (bruises, abrasions, torn clothing). Management requires a multidisciplinary, trauma-informed approach. Priorities: medical stabilization first (ABCs), then forensic examination. Obtain consent before any exam. Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner (SANE) if available. Forensic evidence collection (rape kit): clothing, swabs, fingernail scrapings, hair samples — ideally within 72h. Document injuries with photographs. Labs: STI testing (chlamydia, gonorrhea, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis), pregnancy test, toxicology screen (drug-facilitated assault —GHB, benzodiazepines, ketamine). Empiric treatment: ceftriaxone + doxycycline + metronidazole for STI prophylaxis. Emergency contraception (levonorgestrel 1.5mg PO once). HIV PEP if within 72h. Report to law enforcement (with consent). Arrange safe discharge and follow-up. Psychiatry/crisis counseling referral.

113.title: Drowning
113.caseSummary:
Differential: Ventricular fibrillation, Hypoglycemia

This is an emergency case, so intervention should be done immediately before a physical exam should be done. The patient has a weak pulse, and CPR should be continued. PALS recommends CPR in patients with a heart rate
less than 60 bpm and signs of poor perfusion that does not respond to positive pressure ventilation. The patient does have a weak pulse. There is a risk of inducing ventricular fibrillation with CPR, but most intensive care

professional would start CPR in a patient presenting like this. The airway of the patient should be protected by intubation and ventilation.

The patient has hypothermia which should be corrected. The cold clothes of the patient should be removed, and a warming blanket should be given which will warm the patient. Hypothermic patients are almost always

volume depleted due to cold diuresis, so warm IV fluids should be given. The patient should then be given epinephrine based on the recommendation of Pediatric Advance Life Support (PALS) protocol.

After about 30 minutes of intervention, the patient will begin to recover and CPR can stop. After another 60 minutes, the patient will open her eyes, and the case will end.
113.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a child who was submerged in water, presenting with respiratory distress, hypoxia, altered mental status after water rescue. Drowning = respiratory impairment from submersion in liquid. Outcome: death, survival with morbidity, or survival without morbidity. NOT 'near-drowning' in current terminology. Fresh water vs salt water distinction clinically irrelevant — both cause pulmonary surfactant washout → ARDS. Key: hypoxic brain injury determines prognosis. Management: ABCs, oxygen, BVM or intubation if needed. C-spine precautions if diving mechanism. CXR (pulmonary edema vs aspiration pneumonia). Rewarming if hypothermic. All drowning victims need observation — even asymptomatic can deteriorate (secondary drowning from pulmonary edema). Admit for observation. Prevention counseling.

115.title: Agitation
115.caseSummary:
Differential diagnosis: Substance induced psychotic disorder, Schizophrenia, Psychosis secondary to a medical condition, Delirium, Epileptic seizures, Electrolyte disturbance

This case is similar to the Schizophrenia case, but this case focuses just on correctly treating acute agitation which is a common occurrence in most emergency departments. As the patient has already assaulted a staff
member, IM medication is needed and oral medication does not need to be offered. A typical regimen given is colloquially called the 5-2-1 meaning 5mg of IM Haldol (Haloperidol), 2mg of IM Ativan (Lorazepam), and 1mg
‘of IM Cogentin. As Cogentin IM is very expensive, an alternative is a 5-2-50 which is Smg of IM Haldol, 2mg of IM Ativan (Lorazepam), and 50mg of IM Benadryl (Diphenhydramine). Droperidol and Midazolam can be used
instead of Haldol (it has a shorter half-life than Haldol) and Lorazepam (Lorazepam), but this is not as commonly used. Droperidol has an IM injection, but the USMLE only lists intravenous as an available option, so this is not
the best choice. Once the patient is treated, he will calm down and then labs and a physical exam can be completed. There can be medical causes of acute agitation which should be ruled out, but given the age of the patient

and his presentation, a primary psychiatric diagnosis is likely. Without a history, the exact diagnosis will not be determined in this case.
Other second-generation antipsychotics are available for the treatment of acute agitation which include: IM Olanzapine (Zyprexa), IM Aripiprazole (Abilify), or IM Ziprasidone (Geodon). Haldol is the most commonly
administered in hospital emergency settings due to availability. If Haldol is given, this is typically administered with Lorazepam (Ativan) along with Cogentin or Benadryl to avoid a potential EPS (Extrapyramidal Syndrome)

including dystonias. This can be given while using IM second generation antipsychotics, but not necessary.

Benzodiazepines can be used to treat agitation, but they are not required as most antipsychotics will treat agitation as well as psychosis.
115.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute agitation, aggression, psychomotor activation, and possible threatening behavior. Priority: ensure safety of patient and staff. Determine etiology: psychiatric (schizophrenia, bipolar mania, psychosis) vs substance-induced (stimulants, PCP, alcohol withdrawal) vs medical (hypoglycemia, hypoxia, head injury, sepsis, encephalopathy). Rapid assessment: vital signs, fingerstick glucose, pulse oximetry, brief neuro exam. Verbal de-escalation first-line. If pharmacologic needed: PO preferred over IM if patient willing — lorazepam (benzo) or olanzapine (antipsychotic). If IM required: midazolam + haloperidol or olanzapine IM. Avoid physical restraints unless absolutely necessary — can worsen agitation and cause rhabdomyolysis. If restraints used: 1:1 observation, frequent monitoring. Once stabilized → workup for underlying cause (tox screen, CT head, labs). Psychiatry consult.

118.title: Muscle Pain
118.chiefComplaint: Diffuse muscle pain, dark urine, weakness
118.caseSummary:
Differential: Myocardial infarction, Hematuria, Myopathy
The patient has Rhabdomyolysis due to excessive exercise from running a marathon. The most common presentation is with muscle pain, weakness, and dark urine. In this case, the patient presents with all 3 symptoms. The
key lab value is an elevated CPK level. Inflammation of the liver is also common in Rhabdomyolysis. On urinalysis, the patient will have positive blood but will have few RBC on microscopic examination as myoglobin will make

the dipstick positive.

The treatment for Rhabdomyolysis is fluids. There is no agreed upon regimen, so normal saline, 0.45% normal saline, or lactate ringer can be administered. The patient should then be given bicarbonate to alkalinize the urine

to prevent conversion of myoglobin to methemoglobin. Fluids and waiting are the only effective treatment, Hemodialysis is not necessary in this patient.

‘Once the proper treatment is given, the patient will recover.
118.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with diffuse muscle pain, weakness, dark cola-colored urine (myoglobinuria), and fatigue following prolonged immobilization, crush injury, extreme exertion, or medication reaction. Labs: markedly elevated CK (often >5,000, can be >100,000), elevated Cr (AKI from myoglobin), hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia. UA positive for blood on dipstick but no RBCs on microscopy (myoglobinuria). Rhabdomyolysis = skeletal muscle breakdown → release of intracellular contents (K, phosphate, myoglobin, CK) into bloodstream. Biggest risk: acute kidney injury from myoglobin pigment nephropathy. Management: AGGRESSIVE IV crystalloid resuscitation (NS or LR, 1-2L bolus then 200-300 mL/hr titrated to urine output >200-300 mL/hr). Monitor urine output, renal function, electrolytes (hyperkalemia → cardiac arrhythmia). Alkalinization with bicarb generally NOT recommended. Treat underlying cause.

119.title: Sore Throat
119.caseSummary:
Differential: Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis, Retropharyngeal Abscess, Epiglottitis, Lemierre Syndrome, Lateral Pharyngeal Abscess, Other Bacteria pharyngitis.

This patient has viral pharyngitis. The exact virus will not be determined in the case as it typically is not determined in real life. The main point of the case is to not over-treat. It is important to rule out a Group A Streptococcal

infection by doing a rapid group A strep test. Once negative, give only symptomatic relief with pain medications (ibuprofen or Acetaminophen) along with salt water gargles which has been shown to help.

No other interventions are necessary in this case. In time, the patient will begin to feel better. If you gave antibiotics, you would fail the case. Antibiotics use in viral infections do not help and have led to antibiotic resistance.
119.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with sore throat, cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness, conjunctivitis, and low-grade fever. Viral features (cough, rhinorrhea, conjunctivitis) make strep less likely. Centor criteria: no tonsillar exudates, no tender anterior cervical LAN, cough present, no fever → score 0-1 = no testing needed. Most pharyngitis is viral (adenovirus, rhinovirus, EBV, influenza). Management: supportive care — acetaminophen/NSAIDs, fluids, rest, throat lozenges, salt water gargles. NO antibiotics. Avoid unnecessary antibiotic prescribing — contributes to resistance. If Centor criteria score ≥3 → rapid strep test. If positive → treat as GAS pharyngitis. If negative → supportive only.

120.title: Sore Throat
120.chiefComplaint: Acute sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudates, no cough
120.caseSummary:
Differential: Group C and G Streptococcal Pharyngitis, Retropharyngeal Abscess, Epiglottitis, Infectious mononucleosis, Viral Pharyngitis.

Group A Streptococcal (GAS) is the most common cause of bacterial pharyngitis in children. The physical exam and history are consistent with a bacterial pharyngitis. The patient does not have any viral symptoms such as
congestion or cough. The patient also has a characteristic papular rash along with tonsillar exudates. A rapid strep test should be done as this gives information quickly that will dictate treatment.

Penicillin/Amoxicillin are the treatment of choice for GAS. Alternatives include Cephalosporins (Cephalexin, Cefadroxil, Cefuroxime, Cefpodoxime, Cefdinir, Cefixime), Macrolides (Azithromycin or Clarithromycin), and
Lincosamides (Clindamycin).

Acetaminophen or Tylenol can be administered to treat pain and fever. Once antibiotics are given, the patient will feel better. The patient should be counseled to take the entire regimen of antibiotics to avoid developing

antibiotic resistance.
120.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute sore throat, fever >38°C, tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and NO cough. Centor criteria score ≥3: rapid strep test or throat culture indicated. GAS pharyngitis is most common in children 5-15 years. Treatment: penicillin VK PO x 10 days or amoxicillin (first-line). Single-dose IM benzathine penicillin if adherence concern. Cephalexin or clindamycin if penicillin-allergic. Abx shorten symptoms by 1-2 days and prevent complications: acute rheumatic fever (most important), peritonsillar abscess, and PSGN (though Abx don't prevent PSGN). Patient can return to school 24h after starting antibiotics. Symptomatic: acetaminophen or NSAIDs, fluids. NO aspirin in children (Reye's).

122.title: Painful Rash
122.chiefComplaint: Fever, widespread painful rash, mucosal involvement
122.caseSummary:
Differential: Erythema multiforme, Generalized bullous fixed drug reaction, Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, Linear IgA bullous dermatosis

The patient in this case has Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) from his exposure to Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole. Drug exposure is the most common cause of SJS. The next most common in children is a bacterial infection
with Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Because of this, it is recommended that tests for Mycoplasma pneumoniae to screen for this.

It is important to get bacterial and fungal cultures of the wounds because it is common that patients with SIS will have bacterial infection and sepsis.

The treatment for SJS is mainly supportive. The first thing to do would be to stop the offending agent which in this case would be the Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole. The patient should then be admitted to the ICU and be

given IV fluids and pain medication.

As this patient is presenting in the initial stages of SJS, Cyclosporine should be given as it has been shown to help slow progress of SIS in early stages.
122.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset fever, widespread painful target-like lesions, bullae, epidermal detachment (<10% BSA = SJS, 10-30% = SJS/TEN overlap, >30% = TEN), and mucosal involvement (oral, ocular, genital). Nikolsky sign positive (epidermis sloughs with gentle pressure). Most commonly triggered by medications: sulfa antibiotics, anti-epileptics (lamotrigine, phenytoin, carbamazepine), allopurinol, NSAIDs, within 1-8 weeks of exposure. This is a medical emergency. Immediately discontinue offending drug. Admit to burn ICU. Supportive care: fluid/electrolyte management, wound care, infection prevention, nutritional support, ophthalmology consult. Systemic steroids controversial — not universally recommended. IVIG or cyclosporine may be considered. SCORTEN score for prognosis.

123.title: Leg Pain
123.caseSummary:
Differential: Muscle strain, Cellulitis, venous insufficiency, lymphedema, popliteal cyst.

The patient has classic symptoms of a Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT). The patient has risk factors for a DVT which include: smoking, obesity, tenderness at area of interest, pitting edema, calf swelling 3cm larger than the
other leg, and dilation of superficial veins. The patient would have a High Probability of DVT on the Wells Score.

The D-Dimer results will be elevated. This would be optional since the patient has a high probability due to risk factors of having a DVT. A calf ultrasound (doppler) should be done to confirm the diagnosis. The patient should
then be put on anticoagulants. The options for anticoagulation are: LMW herparin (Lovenox) + Warfarin (Coumadin) OR Lovenox + dabigatran OR Lovenox + edoxaban OR Rivaroxaban monotherapy OR Apixaban
Monotherapy. The patient should be counseled on smoking cessation and put on a weight loss diet.
